Now begins the *avamarśa* juncture (*sandhi*), which consists of the convergence of the *prakarī* (minor incident) and the *niyatāpti* (certainty of attainment).

It is indicated in the sixth act: therein, that for which a result is envisioned solely for the sake of another, yet which is devoid of a further consequence (*anubandha*), one should designate as a *prakarī*. And here, it is the unextended activity of Hanumān.

The burning of Laṅkā and so forth; and there is also the lack of pervasion (*avyāptatva*), because Hanumān’s actions, like Sugrīva’s, are for the most part not explicitly described. "The certainty of the accomplishment of the task [is] through the absence of obstacles;
it is that which brings about the necessary attainment. And that [certainty] is—[dependent on] one who is subject to the power of his mass of arms.
And so forth; "this [was done] by a mere human" (4), and so forth;
"something [was done] by monkeys" (5), and so forth.

Through the persistence of these two, the mutual connection of the thirteen subsidiary elements, beginning with the exception (apavāda), is the juncture of reflection (avamarsa-sandhi). And that [juncture] is defined as: "Where one should reflect due to anger, or due to calamity, or due to seduction..."
"That reflective awareness (avamarśa) is said to have the meaning of a seed whose embryo has burst forth" (6);
"whose embryo has burst forth" means directed toward the fruit. That...
And: beginning with "Is the youngest son consecrated? and ending with "What of it?";
beginning with "The insult to the banner of the Thunderbolt-bannered [Indra]" and ending with "the arrows";
and beginning with "of those who have performed deeds and counter-deeds," and so forth.

Its constituent parts are as follows: "In that regard, there are Apavāda (denial), Saṃpheṭa (collision), Vidrava (flight), Drava (melting), Śakti (power), Dyuti (splendor), Prasaṅga (consequence), Chalanam (evasion), Vyavasāya (resolve), and Nirodhanam (obstruction)."
"Excitement, agitation, and grasping—these are the thirteen.
(11) "Burnt," and so forth. "By familiarity" means by contact.
"Existing in the mass" (piṇḍasthāni) means existing in the very gold-mass that serves as their cause;
for every effect, even when destroyed, persists in its cause alone. "Wagging the tail" (utpucchayamāne) means shaking the tail.
In the word *sati*, the suffix *ṇiṅ* is used in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) according to the rule beginning with *pucchabhāṇḍa*. *Uddeśāḥ* means sections (*pradeśāḥ*). By this—
An excess of burning sensation is indicated. (14)//1//

"His own," and so forth. *Rūpa* refers to forms such as blue, yellow, and so on; *karman* refers to ritual actions such as the svastika and so on; and *śilpa* refers to craftsmanship. "From the result" (*phalataḥ*) means from dissolution or from being reduced to ashes; the verbal root is *ñi phalā* in the sense of "dissolution. Within the flames of various colors, "these... [the text continues].
The meaning is that it is impossible to distinguish [them], thinking, "These are the rays of the jewel; these are the flames. //2//
"doḥsandoha... and so forth.

*Vaśaṃvadāḥ* means obedient; [according to the rule] "the suffix *khac* is applied after *priya* and *vaśa* when followed by *vada*" (Pāṇini 3.2.38). Due to the pride of prosperity (*sampadgarveṇa*), *sarvaṅkaṣaḥ* means one who oppresses all (*sarvabādhakaḥ*).

By the rule "sarvakūla" (Pāṇini 4.2.75), the suffix *khac* is applied. *Amarāvatī* is the city of Indra; the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule "matau bahvaco'najirādīnām" (Pāṇini 6.3.119). It is [so called] because that city has him as its presiding deity (*adhidevatā*).
By the word *markaṭaka*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of smallness (*alpārtha*).
"Daiva" means pertaining to the gods. "Āvaśyakam" (necessity) is used with the particle "dhik.
The sense is that for Rāvaṇa, who possesses only physical prowess, disaster from Rāma—who is endowed with both divine and human power—is already a certainty. //3//
"This is nothing [extraordinary]," he says; the sense is that because of his immoral conduct and other such factors, he will fall into even greater calamities than these.
From "Starting from here... up to "...make the bee-like Śrī limping" (20), this is the dramatic element called *apavāda* (defamation), because it proclaims the faults of Rāvaṇa;
as it has been said: "Defamation (*apavāda*) consists in the proclamation of faults. (21)
"Āḥ, O descendant of Pulastya," and so forth.
"Ā" is used here to express affliction; as Amarasimha states: "Āstu may be used in the sense of anger and affliction."

It was a source of sorrow that even though the purity of the field was lacking because he was the son of a *rākṣasī*, the purity of the seed— which is the cause of discipline— was also rendered futile.
"Vidyā," and so forth: there are fourteen sciences (*vidyā*), consisting of the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra, and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*). (23)
The four Vedas were his own fixed portion, while the remaining ten branches of knowledge belonged to his *praṇaptṛ*—that is, his grandson’s son—because [Viśravas] was the son of Viśravas;
[the latter] being dull-witted (*jaḍa*), that is, ignorant. (24)

"Jaḍa" means "ignorant," according to Amara. "How? expresses astonishment: even though you possess knowledge—which is the cause for the continued occurrence of effects even when the causal conditions are present—and which is superior even to that of Brahmā, how has this engagement with an improper path arisen? This is astonishing. //4//
"And having stood for a moment" means that his silence was for the purpose of reflecting upon the preceding and subsequent actions.
He says this very thing with the words "How can it be so? and so forth. Akṣa is the son of Rāvaṇa. //5//

*durvihitam* means *durvidhānam* (a bad arrangement), with the suffix *kta* used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). *Upālabhyālam* means "let there be no reproach"; here the suffix *ktvā* is used according to the rule *alaṃ-khalvoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.18). How do we understand this? [The answer is: *vibhāṣā*.

Regarding the rule "kathami liṅ ca" (Pāṇini 3.3.143), the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*) for deliberation (*sampradhāraṇā*); deliberation means the consideration of what ought to be done. "To practice" (*caritum*) means "to know," for all roots meaning motion have the sense of knowing.

By that very "foot"—characterized by departure, such as perspiration, sighing, and so forth, or by the physical foot itself; for it is said: "The word *pada* is used in the senses of resolve, protection, place, mark, foot, and object. (30)
Thus says Amara.

This refers to the characteristic of arriving at that very moment. Does this arrival come directly from the camp (*kaṭaka*) itself, and not after resting at one's own home or elsewhere? The word *kaccit* is used here as an interrogative particle.
"Rāmarājadhānī": by this, he describes the security of the camp and the abundance of its resources.
"With intent" (*sākūtam*) means that the slaying of Rāvaṇa is certain; this is the intended meaning.
"Standing rigidly" (*stabdha sthitvā*): the rigidity (*stambha*) is caused precisely by this. "Fearlessly" (*niḥśaṅkam*): here, fear (*śaṅkā*)...
"Caused by the fear of the king arising from the report of bad news";
*saṃyamya* = having bound;
*upagṛhya* = having taken hold of; *puraskṛtya* = having honored with garments, ornaments, and so forth.

"Exaltedness" (*udāttatā*) is the quality called "fullness" (*pūrṇatva*); the meaning is that it exists as long as the substance does, being innate and unconditional; the implication is that it is not merely occasional. Regarding the phrase "by way of distinction" (*viśeṣeṇa*), etc.: its loftiness...
The meaning is that it is well-known in the world.
Regarding the phrase "without distinction" and so forth: by saying "he worships," he intends [the practice] to be continuous.
By the word *udara*, he intends the state of being a son. Regarding "insufficient" and so forth:
this refers to forming an expectation without making a distinction between one's own [resources] and those of others.
The quality known as familiarity and continuity is insufficient— that is, very slight— when compared to other rogues.
If this very [conduct] belongs to the virtuous,
it is somehow sweet because it has not been produced [by effort], meaning it is limitless; indeed, the base proceed with partiality, whereas the virtuous—
The sense is that they are "equally [beneficial] to all. Alternatively, this is the quality of the virtuous:
it is "unlimited" (*aparyāpta*), meaning it is without end; the meaning is that the virtuous always and everywhere provide assistance.
Here, the first half-verse serves as the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).

This is the ornament called *dṛṣṭānta* (the example), which occurs when the reason—namely, the absence of partiality—is observed in the *sapakṣa* (the similar instance), such as the night-lily (*kumuda*), while "this" [the speaker] is the subject to be proven as being virtuous.
As it has been said: "The observation of the reason in the *sapakṣa* is the *dṛṣṭānta* for the sake of establishing the probandum" (31). //6//
"I too do not know" was said because the news from other spies must remain unknown to the other [spy];
as it has been stated by Kāmandaka: "One should dispatch spies."
"At sacred fords, one should not recognize oneself or others as belonging to heretical sects and the like, nor should they recognize one another as such. (32) Thus [it is said].
"One's own kin" (*svakulyam*) means those born of one's own family.
*Pramohaḥ* [is so called] because of the onset of suffering.
*Āryasantānaḥ* refers to the son of Pulastya. In the reading *ārdrasantānaḥ*, it means one whose mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) is moistened by compassion. Regarding *jyāyāṃsam*: "equal to a father."
The word "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) is the reason why he must not be transgressed against. "How so? is a question regarding the cause for his abandonment.
[The text says: "Ask Daśagrīva. It was not Vibhīṣaṇa who abandoned him, but rather—

The implication is that Vibhīṣaṇa alone has been abandoned. Alternatively, "it is fate": the meaning is that this is the wicked deed of Fate (vidhi) itself, which intends to make him experience great suffering, and not the fault of Rāvaṇa; for [as it is said]: "The intellect..."
In response to the doubt that "this is a method for concealing the mantra, following one's own karma," he says: "If [the recipient] is worthy of hearing it,
[then] 'This is your king.'"
Because he does not accept his own teaching and possesses a distorted intellect, there is a statement of indifference; as it was said by Maitryā: "They meditate upon me..."

"Compassion for those who are happy and those who are suffering, sympathetic joy toward those who perform meritorious deeds, and equanimity toward those of wrong views. (34) Thus, "avaṣṭabdha" means supported or relied upon; [he] this...
The ellipsis of the sentence is "one should abandon.
Prostration is a constituent part of the prayer,
or it is for the purpose of avoiding fear induced by the expression of [the king's] majesty.
The sense is that it is improper for a human and a monkey [to mate].
Regarding the phrase "jātim" and so forth:
*mānuṣīm* means born of Manu; the suffix *ṅīp* is applied [to form the feminine]. (35)

Hehaya is Kārtavīrya. "Not now" means it is not proper; since the sense is that of fitness (*arha*), the suffix *tumun* is used according to the rule *śakadhṛṣa-* (Pāṇini 3.4.65). He reminds us of the two stages of the sacrifice: the preparation of the materials and the binding of the sacrificial post. The address "O descendant of Pulastya" is a statement regarding his lack of valor, while "the great performer of the Agnihotra" refers to [his own status].

And "the enjoyers of the sacrifice" (kratubhuj) refers to the cause of liberation. Sītā is merely the gateway; the ultimate goal, however, is the protection of the deity—this is the intended meaning. *Kārā* means a prison.
The term *kārā* is a conventional expression (nipāta) meaning "imprisonment.
Because this [expression] takes the form of a request, it is the ornament known as *anunaya* (entreaty);
as it has been said: "An entreaty (*abhyarthanā*), however, is declared to be *anunaya*."
By means of sweet words. (38) Thus, [verse] 7.

"What shall I say? and so forth. What shall I say? The meaning is that it cannot be described. Having grasped the middle portion of the mountains with his hand turned downward, while his head and shoulders were held upward.
When it is seized, there is the occurrence of friction against the top of the forearm;
even with such friction against the top, only a mere hair's breadth is destroyed—thus he speaks of the firmness of the armlet. Envy.
The object is loftiness. "Softness" is due to its being newly sprouted.
In the phrase "with their heads," the instrumental case is used in a figurative sense (*upalakṣaṇe*). (39) "Even the weight": it cannot bear even the weight of the arms.
The meaning of the word "api" (also/even) is: how much more so [the acts] such as uprooting and the like? //8//
"Even the adversary" (*vipakṣam api*): the particle *api* is used here in the sense of censure. The meaning is that even resorting to an adversary by abandoning one's kin is censurable.
"How [could this have been done] by you yourself? and so forth.

The example by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is the locus for the certain determination of the absence of the probans through the absence of the probandum; this is because of the etymological derivation:

*dṛṣṭaḥ* (seen/observed) and *antaḥ* (end/determination), as in the Amarakośa: "The word *anta* [is used] in the sense of a conclusion, death, essential nature, certainty, and proximity. By that [definition]:
This is established through inference. (41) The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
the person under discussion must be one who abstains from seizing the wives of others and so forth, because he is free from calamity.
Like Vibhīṣaṇa; he who does not turn away from evil falls into calamity, like Rāvaṇa.
Thus, seeing you destroyed root and branch by your own commission of evil—

The meaning is that the world will turn away from unjust acts. "With entreaty" means that because one who is addicted to vices is not an object of acceptance for oneself, there is an entreaty [to prevent them].
"Regarding the phrase *ariṣaḍvarga* and so forth: a group of six is a *ṣaḍvarga*; that which belongs to enemies (*ari*) is thus called the *ariṣaḍvarga*.
And those [enemies], beginning with desire (*kāma*), are the "feet" because they are the causes of wandering and are the roots of calamity. Even a single one..."
The primary [object]; the sense is that desire alone, being mentioned first, is what must be abandoned.
"Bhramarīm" (the female bee); it also suggests one who is habitually wandering. "Khañjaḥ" = one whose feet are impaired.
The implication is that in the absence of the restoration of Sītā, there would be the loss of the kingdom;

as it is stated by Kāmandaka: "The disclosure of secrets, inciting one's own faction toward improper acts, jealousy, anger, intolerance, hostility, and recklessness—these and other such things arise from addiction to women."
And that which was previously proclaimed:
therefore, the king [should avoid] addiction to women.
One who desires sovereignty should renounce [these]. (42) Thus. (9)
"Arrayed" means occupied. The construction is: "If anything remains, then it must be Vibhīṣaṇa alone.
"Child," "of the two," and so forth.

Because the application of means is inappropriate when the true nature of the two persons situated on the two sides of the camp is not understood; as it has been said: "Having known the nature of the enemy and oneself, one should employ conciliation and the other [means]. (43)
From "starting from here" up to "he would become one whose purpose is greatly slackened" (44), this section—
consisting of the contrivance of a breach between friends— is the subsidiary element (*upāṅga*) called "Breach" (*bheda*), which is a type of juncture (*sandhi*).
As it has been said: "But the division [of enemies] comes from the fabrication of dissension among friends through deceitful talk.
(45) What is appropriate now? The word "what" (*kim*) is a question regarding the means (*upāya*).
Because Rāma’s honor had been diminished by the abduction of his wife, he lacked the primary quality of friendliness;

because of his skill in reasoning and refutation, and because Rāvaṇa was of a firm and haughty nature, conciliation (*sāman*) was shown to be inappropriate due to his aversion to pleasant speech— these being the reasons previously stated for Rāma.
Furthermore, due to the absence of greed and other such passions, he was beyond the scope of bribery;
and because he had conquered Rāvaṇa and Kārtavīrya, defeated Bhārgava, and slain Vālin, and because he possessed great allies, he was beyond the reach of military force.
Because he was endowed with superhuman power acquired through the instructions of Viśvāmitra,
there was no occasion for the employment of magic or sorcery;
and because he never engaged in any activity contrary to the principles of righteousness, he was not to be disregarded.
Having determined this,
he introduces the remaining means, namely *bheda* (sowing dissension), beginning with the words "the prince," and so forth. As it has been said:

Kāmandakī: One should win over a person whose primary disposition is friendship and who possesses a virtuous mind through conciliation; one should win over a greedy person and one who is impoverished by honoring them.

"One should bring them under control through gifts. (46) Furthermore, those who are susceptible to division are mentioned in that very same place: "One who has been falsely accused, one who desires wealth, one who has been summoned but not honored, one who hates the king, and one born of the king's own lineage..."

One who is hated by the king, one who engages in harmful transactions, one who is appointed to a judicial office, one who is fond of battle, one who is reckless, one who is self-conceited, and one whose virtue, desire, and wealth have been severed— [these are those who should not be questioned].
Enraged, insulted by honor or dishonor,
deprived of wealth and wife,
and longing for great enjoyments.

"One whose external kinsmen are exhausted, whose external wealth is gone, and who has been cast out"— thus are the persons to be divided [from the circle] fully described. (47) Here, by the term "prince" (*rājaputra*), his noble lineage, his desire for fortune, and his longing for great enjoyments are indicated,
as well as his worthiness for honor.

And being honored for one's truthfulness is included [among the qualities]. By the word "this one" (*asau*), which refers back to the subject at hand, the state of being a crown prince (*yuvarāja*) is stated as the cause of division;

as it has been said: "The minister and the crown prince—these two are the arms of the lord of the earth. One should strive to create a rift between the counselor, the minister, and the family priest."

"When they are divided, the powerful crown prince will likewise be divided. (48) By the word "child" (*bāla*), his engagement in harmful conduct due to a lack of discrimination between what is beneficial and what is detrimental is expressed; for this very reason, he is "of immature intellect," meaning his intellect is incapable of critical analysis (*akṣodakṣama*).
"Skilled in non-removal and non-addition" means precisely this:
therefore, like an unbaked earthen vessel, it "sucks up"—that is, it drinks—water and so forth. For that [vessel] indeed [drinks] water and the like.
He drinks quickly.
"The two enemies of his father"—this is an intensification of the enmity; "having consecrated."

The display of fruits such as sovereignty [is for the purpose of] being led away— that is, being removed. The sense is that [the mind] is slackened and so forth, because one's own true purpose must be pursued.
"Endow him with power.
By speaking these words preceded by a smile, the weakness of the one being addressed has been indicated.
He states that very point with the words beginning "What more," etc., [referring to] "the one in the form of an embryo."

By means of the term *rūpa* (form), he sets aside that which is conveyed by the word *bāla* (child)— a term denoting a lack of independence caused by extreme youth— by using the word *abhinava* (fresh/new).
Because he did not exist previously, his radiance arises from being the object of Sugrīva’s affection; for this very reason, there is the expression "cherished. By this—

He renders the term "king" (rāja) devoid of [other] scope by means of the words "and those who belong to him. This is because Sugrīva’s kinship with the Aṅgadas is due to his being the husband of Tārā; thus, they are indeed the relatives of Sugrīva as well.
The interpretation: "Rising up" means having set out upon an improper path;
by this, he excludes [the possibility of] external kinsmen and the like.
This refers to the thought: "The task must be accomplished by breaking the limbs."

The ornament called "contradiction" (viparyaya) arises because the subsequent statements alter the reflection and deliberation [of the opponent's position]; as it has been said: "the alteration of the deliberation."
"There may be a reversal of judgment. (53) Thus it is said. Regarding the phrase "one who considers the time," Kāmandaka says here: "At night, the owl kills..."
Just as a crow watches for a crow and an owl watches for the end of the night, so should one set out after observing the proper time;
for it is at the right time that actions bear fruit in this world.
"Desired things. (54) The sense is that this is the wrong time.
He says the same thing with the words "with great enthusiasm," and so forth.
By this, devotion and affection for the master are expressed. *Upatyakāḥ* refers to the regions near the base of a mountain.

The status of *rāma* as the object (*karman*) is established by the rule *adhi-śīṅ* (Pāṇini 1.4.46). This is because, although Rāvaṇa lacked the strength of arms due to being defeated by Vālin, he possessed the strength of a fortress (*durga-bala*) as his support, which was removed by the construction of the bridge; furthermore, [the action] was for the purpose of building that bridge.
The sense is that because [the enemy] has already been largely conquered, it is the wrong time for the employment of expedients, given the expectation of Sugrīva’s assistance.
He expresses this very point in the verse beginning with "asau" (he).
"Even by all the worlds"—that is to say, by everyone—because such a state has been reached by the Great Hero due to the wonder of Mālyavat’s reflection. "Ah! (expresses astonishment).
In distress. //10//
"Of Paulastya," and so forth. *Nirmālya* means that which has been used and discarded—that is, unfit for consumption.
In the word *kurvāṇena*, the suffix *śānac* is used in the sense of cause (equivalent to "for the purpose of"); it means "for the sake of performing.
*Unmudrayati* means "he causes to blossom" or "he causes to unfold."
The sense is that even such radiance as this did not exist previously;
[this refers to] the return of the *rasa*.

Because they have returned to their natural state; the sense is that these two [the eyes] become clear due to the departure of the enemy's strength and the joy arising from the certainty of Rāvaṇa’s death. *Svadante* means they become sweet. //11//

*Pārṣṇiḥ* means the rear region. (57) By this, it is stated that even though Rāvaṇa had conquered the three worlds, he possessed the power of energy (*utsāha-śakti*) because he performed the duty of an attacker.
(58) *Sākṣāt* means that Sugrīva was indeed assisted by Rāma himself.
By the statement regarding "friendliness toward what must be done" (*kāryamaitrī*), the power of sovereignty (*prabhuśakti*) consisting of treasury and army is described.
By the verse beginning with "Hanūmat," etc., the power of sovereignty consisting of knowledge of one's own and the enemy's forces is described.
The power of mantras has been described. For this very reason, he says "well-prepared," and so forth. "About to advance" (*abhiyāsyan*) means intending to go for the sake of conquering the enemy;
regarding this, Kāmandaka says: "With his rear cleared and piercing [the enemy] from the front..."

"Knowing the enemy's actions and aware of the places of danger, he should enter the earth [the battlefield] with an army that is pure and strong in its own resources, remaining vigilant against the foe. (61) *Āsāra* = reinforcement.
The "Power of Allies" (mitrabala):
from "one's own substance" (*ātmadravya*) up to "the seeker of victory" (*vijigīṣu*), this is the aphorism of Auśanasa.
The meaning of this is as follows: self-perfection (*ātmasampat*) is energy (*utsāha*); perfection of resources (*dravyasampat*) is the power of sovereignty (*prabhuśakti*);

and perfection of constituents (*prakṛtisampat*) is the power of counsel (*mantraśakti*). For this very reason, these constitute the foundation of policy (*naya*). An illustration of this is its point of demonstration; namely, the qualities of one desirous of victory (*vijigīṣuguṇāḥ*).
The meaning is that all [these things] exist.
"Stupefaction" (stambha) arises from the suffering caused by the excellence of Rāmabhadra’s virtues.
He states this very point in the passage beginning with "yat tasmin," etc. "In him" (tasmin) refers to the one possessed of the strength of his arms.
The "inferior ones" (*kṣudrāḥ*) are those whose strength is less than that of Vālin. "In the same way" (*tathaiva*) means as before.
Since we remain entirely unharmed, therefore the strength of a fortress (*durgabala*) is a strength even greater than the strength of one's own arms (*bhujabala*).
The sense is that this has been understood.
He says "by a mortal," and so forth, to show that even that [victory] has already passed away;
"vijitvarāḥ" means those whose nature is to conquer.

The suffix *kvarap* is applied after the roots *iṇ*, *naś*, *ji*, and *sṛt*. For one possessing such qualities, the ocean is already as good as crossed. "For" (*hi*) means "because. Two hundred *gavyūtis* equal four hundred *krośas*. How much indeed is that?

The phrase "only a very little" refers to Rāma’s enthusiasm; according to Amarasimha, "a gavyūti is a female [measure] equal to two krośas. There is sorrow because Rāvaṇa was slain immediately after the leaping. And those are the qualities.
As stated by Kāmandaka: noble birth, service to the elderly, enthusiasm, generosity, knowledge of the mind, intelligence, boldness, and truthfulness.
Absence of procrastination, lack of stinginess, humility, self-reliance, knowledge of place and time, firmness,
endurance of all afflictions, and omniscience.
Skillfulness, vigor, secrecy of counsel, reliability, heroism,
knowledge of devotion, and gratitude.
Affection for those who have come for refuge, impatience with wrongdoing, lack of fickleness, having seen the scriptures through one's own practice, skillfulness,
and far-sightedness.
Endurance of fatigue, eloquence of speech, having a non-cruel retinue,
and natural expansiveness.
The emergence of virtues in one who desires victory. (66) Thus [ends the section]. 12.
"Afflicted by thirst," and so forth. *Tarṣa* means thirst (*pipāsā*);
by the affliction thereof, [the flames] are "licking repeatedly," that is, licking one another again and again.
"With tongues"; this is the inherent nature of thirst.

"With cries" (*ravyaiḥ*) means "possessing cries" (*ravavadbhiḥ*); [this is formed] by the rule stating that in the section on the suffix *ya*, it should be stated that [the suffix] is seen after other [roots] as well.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the qualities of snow and so forth" (68), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) implies the *yaP* suffix.

In the form *vyatilelihānā*, the suffix *ānaC* is applied according to the rule "the [suffix] *ānaC* is used for the agent when there is a reciprocal action" (70) from the *yaṅ*-luṅ form (69). She [suckles] with eight [teats], because she drinks from two breasts. She...
Even though she has been raised in such a manner, what will she see regarding her son? What suffering will she witness? How will she witness it?
[She will witness] such affliction.
The remainder [of the verse] implies that Rāvaṇa is indeed slain. //13//

Regarding the phrase "śāntaṃ pratihatam" (it is pacified, it is struck down): the suffix *kta* is used here according to the rule "āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca" (Pāṇini 3.3.132), meaning "may it be pacified. Thus, the sense is "let it become calm."
The ellipsis is "an inauspicious omen feared for [her] existence.
Regarding "those who fear misfortune": this is a fear born of love; as it has been said—"Love perceives dangers even where there is no cause. (73)
"Array of arms," and so forth. *Vihaṅgikā* means a carrying-pole (*bhārayaṣṭi*).

(74) *Guṇas* mean virtues such as heroism, and also ropes. (75) By the term "ten-necked one" (*daśakandhara*), he expresses the capacity for bearing a heavy load. *Dhurīṇe* means a bearer; [the suffix] *khaḥ* [is applied here]. (76)

In the phrase *sarvadhurād* (Pāṇini 5.1.2), the suffix *kha* is applied by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) based on the word *kha*. Even so, if there is a failure [in governance], the sense is that this is the inherent nature of kingship (*rājya*) and not the fault of the king. //14//
The obstruction of tears [is removed] by comforting Sāraṇa.
"Knowing," and so forth;
as if it had turned away.
The sense is that misfortunes are being experienced.
First, I do not say of myself that I am unfortunate in the sense of being the cause of the family's survival;
the ellipsis is "I am unfortunate, [but] not the cause of the family's survival."

[This is] the state of affairs. However, if the seed for the funeral offering (*nivāpabīja*)—that is, the cause for the satisfaction of our lineage—should remain [in our family], then it would be solely by the fortune of the great-souled Viśravas; such is the meaning. In the reading *naḥ kulam*, it is not [the case that the seed remains].

I say: the word "related by family" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. If, through the power of Viśravas’s asceticism, the seed for the funeral offering were to remain undifferentiated, it would indeed remain so.
This is the meaning.
The sense is that, due to misfortune, the conceit of possessiveness (*mamatābhimāna*) shall perish. //15//
The tossing of the banner arises from the agitation caused by the occurrence of a great calamity.
"Prahasta," and so forth.
"Uparudhya" means having surrounded or besieged.

The monkeys alone are the entire ocean; the meaning is that only monkeys are seen, and no other entity exists. Just as the world sinks into a single ocean, so too does Laṅkā—this is the sense. Of the news...
In brief, he spoke of Rāma’s swiftness of action, his superior victory, and his own dire peril. //16//
Of the "group of objects of cognition" (*prameyagrāmasya*), that is, of the collection of things to be known;
"reflecting the face" (*yathāmukhīnam*) means showing a reflection similar to the face;
the meaning is "excellent. This alone constitutes the excellence of the mirror.
The meaning is that the elders perceive the very essence of the matter.
Regarding the term *yathāmukha*—meaning "a reflection similar to the face"—it is derived in the sense of "that in which [the face] is seen," according to the rule *yathāmukhasammukha*. (78)

By such [statements], the suffix *kha* is applied; furthermore, even though the word *yathā* has the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*), it forms an *avyayībhāva* compound as in *yathāmukha*, due to a specific grammatical rule (*nipātana*). (79)
Adīrghasūtratā means acting quickly; it signifies necessity, that is to say, the cause. According to Amarasimha, "dīrghasūtra" means one who acts slowly.
Kiṃvidhāna means what kind of action.
"Having heard," and so forth.
*Ardhe* means "some";
its status as a pronominal (*sarvanāman*) is established by the rule *prathamacarama* (Pāṇini 1.1.33).
They wipe away or draw out from the sheath; the verbal root is *uñch* in the sense of "removing.
*Kaukṣeyaka* means a sword; [the suffix] *ḍhakañ* is applied according to the rule beginning with *kulakukṣi*. In the half [verse].
Furthermore, "in the same way" means as in the previous state;
"that" refers to the means for propitiating Sītā;
this is the subsidiary element (upāṅga) called *citra*, which is a sub-division of the juncture (*sandhyantara*).
As it has been said: "The delineation of form is manifold. (84) //17//

"Saiva" means precisely that which pertains to the state of being established in one's own nature (*svasthāvasthā*). "Parispandamudrā" is the manner of restlessness or agitation. "Gopura" is a city gate;
that which pertains to it by way of being its protector is "gaulmīna," meaning connected to a *gulma* (a military outpost or guard station). A *gulma* is so named—

The specific numerical measure of a *bala* is as follows: nine elephants, nine chariots, twenty-seven horses, and forty-five foot soldiers; [this is called] "one elephant, one chariot" (*ekebhaikaratha*).

Three horses constitute a *patti*, and five *pattis* constitute a *senāmukha*. By multiplying all these units by three in successive order, the designations for the higher formations—*gulma* and *gaṇa*—are explained. (85)
Thus says Amara.
By such a commander of the forces, distinguished by many divisions (*gulma*),
[the gate] should be constructed.
*Maryādā* means a restriction; the sense is the prevention of an enemy's entry.
Its downward orientation is due to the unspeakability of death.
"Alas, my child," and so forth.
"This is death.
The accusative case is used here in the sense of "extreme connection" (*atyantasaṃyoga*) with the word *kāla*.
The intended meaning is: "This very thing has become the fruit of his long life. The word "how? (*katham*) expresses grief (*kheda*).
He addresses those who have fled with the words beginning "Turn back" (*vyāvartadhvam*), etc. "Turn back" means "return.
"Attend" (*upādhvam*) means "serve. "Consisting of missiles" (*astramayīm*) means having the form of weapons; [the name] "Jayā."
This has been stated in the *Laghustuti*: "Lakṣmī in the royal court, Jayā at the front of battle," and so forth.
By the word *paśu* (beast), he expresses a lack of heroism. The middle one is Paulastya, namely Kumbhakarṇa; [the meaning is] that even now there is fear of Rāma.
The meaning is "there is not," as indicated by the tone;
however, according to the literal wording, it means "there is fear" in order to speak of the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa.
Śāradā indicates that this is what is intended to be expressed. //18//

The indeclinable *svasti* is used here in the sense of a benediction. By the proximity of the verb "may they be victorious" (*vijayetām*), Śāradā indicates that Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa are the agents of victory, even though this was not intended by Mālyavat.

"Agrejam ityādi" and so forth. The construction is: "Whom will he consecrate first, due to his heroism—the elder brother or the younger? [He will consecrate] Rāvaṇa by way of his own lineage (bhāva), and Vibhīṣaṇa by way of his own absence (abhāva); respectively, upon his [Rāvaṇa's] persistence or destruction.
The sense is that there shall be freedom from obstacles for the kingdom of Rāvaṇa and Vibhīṣaṇa; by this, he introduces the defeat of Kumbhakarṇa. //19//

He says that very thing: "Do not fear," and so forth. "Fear" refers to that which is produced by excessive gravity; the sense is: "Let it not be," because of its non-existence. Regarding the benediction, the rule *māṅi luṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.175) applies, and by the rule *na māṅyoge* (Pāṇini 6.4.74), there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.
*Vaiśeṣika* means "distinguished" (*viśiṣṭa*). That which is distinguished is a *viśeṣa*;
that which is precisely a *viśeṣa* is a *vaiśeṣika*. The suffix *ṭhak* is applied in the sense of the base itself according to Pāṇini 4.3.74 (*vinayādibhyaṣṭhak*).

The meaning is that there is no burden greater than the previous one. However, the contingency of an excessive burden would arise if the entire aggregate of Kumbhakarṇa’s limbs were to fall; that alone—
He says "it does not exist" with the words beginning "the two mountain-like arms," and so forth. The term "mountain-like" (*śailau*) expresses an excess of weight.

"Utksipnunā" means by one who is impelling upwards; the suffix *knu* is applied according to the rule "from the roots *tras*, *gṛdh*, *dhṛṣ*, and *kṣip*, [the suffix] *knu*" (Pāṇini 3.2.140). "Laghukṛtam" means made light.

By means of the suffix *cvi*, he states that when the collection of parts falls, there is excessive weight (*atigaurava*), whereas when that very same [collection] falls disintegrated, that [weight] is absent. The sense is: because it falls lightly, there is no excess of burden.

From "starting from here" up to "we breathe just as before" (93), this constitutes the dramatic element named *vidrava* (flight/distress), consisting of forms such as killing and imprisonment; as it has been said: "*vidrava* is killing, imprisonment, and so forth" (94).
The genitive case in "jīvato rāmasya" is used in the sense of disregard (anādare); the meaning is "disregarding the living Rāma.
"Viṣayīkṛtam" means "seen," that is to say, "ascertained."

"Anāśvasitavya" means that which is not a means for gaining confidence; the suffix -tavya is used here in the sense of the instrument (karaṇa) by virtue of the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.113).
"What now?"—
the meaning is that it is only as before, not something new.
This [is said] because of the abduction of Sītā.

The determination of the cause (*hetvavadhāraṇa*)—namely, the ascertainment of the action that takes the form of Rāvaṇa’s misfortune—is a subsidiary element (*upāṅga*) called *sandhyantara*. As it has been said:
"The determination of the cause is considered to be the ascertainment of a matter by means of a reason" (97).

The *vaihāsikās* are those whose purpose is jesting (98). They mock [the characters] by imagining that such words as "Do not fear" (99) and so forth are the speech of Rāvaṇa; this is the intended meaning.
"Yadi," and so forth.

"Prahāsayuktā bibhīṣikā" refers to a terrifying figure made of grass or similar materials, such as a representation of a man or beast intended to frighten others. Valor is manifested through battle, and not otherwise.
This was a terrifying display in the form of joking words; therefore, for you who have not yet conquered Indra’s son (Indrajit),
this jest brings no fear.
This is the state of affairs; by this, he introduces the defeat of Indrajit.
He says that very thing in the passage beginning with "sannaddha" and so forth.

Here, the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consists in propitiating through fire-oblation (*homa*) the Sun, Mars, and others who obstruct the rains. By "malevolent planet" (*duṣṭagraha*) is meant a cruel planet (*krūragraha*).
And by the phrase "due to persistent attachment," it means that by Śakrajit,
who was equipped with a fully drawn rainbow, [the city was besieged].
And he seized— that well-known rain in the form of a succession of arrows from the gods of great exertion— which had its vajra-weapons ready. "Ava-jagṛhe" means it was obstructed.
*Avagraha* means the obstruction of rain;
this very [obstruction], consisting of weapons— that is, abounding in arms— [was directed] toward that sacrificer of heroes, who was indeed a hero.

"In which [the earth] there was a sacrificer" (yajvā)—that is, one who performed sacrifices (*yajamāna*). The feminine suffix *ṅīp* is prohibited here by the rule *ano bahuvrīheḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.12). "Sacrifice" (*iṣṭi*) means, in this context, battle.
"Completely pacified" (*samupaśamita*) means both propitiated and slain. He by whom Indra was conquered—Indra himself was also slain.

This is the meaning. *Diṣṭyā* is an indeclinable used in the sense of joy; it means "we are satisfied. (22) *Nirduḥkha* means as if free from suffering; [it refers to one] by the force of suffering...
The meaning is that, with a paralyzed mind, one does not experience its consequences (*tadanubhāvāt*).
"In calamity" (*vyatikare*) means in misfortune; the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "Misfortune (*vyasana*) is also calamity (*vyatikara*)" (104).
"Utterly destroying" (*samūlaghātam*) means together with the roots; this is according to the rule beginning with "with *samūla* and *akṛta*" (Pāṇini 3.4.36). (105)

The suffix *ṇamul* [is applied]; according to the rule "in the case of *kaṣa* and others, there is a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*) according to the specific form [of the root]," and that is for the purpose of conveying the means (*sādhana*), person (*puruṣa*), number (*saṅkhyā*), and tense (*kāla*).
Even though he strikes us—that is, afflicts us—we live just as before, as if we were in a state of happiness.
The rows of celestial palaces are overwhelmed—that is, covered—by the ocean of grief born from death, such as that caused by Narāntaka and others;
for even the ocean is swallowed up by the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni). By this [it is shown].
An excess of both anger and sorrow has been expressed; it also flashes forth [in the mind] as being for the sake of victory over the son of Daśaratha.
For the thorough cleansing—that is, the liberation from limiting adjuncts—of the self, that is, the living soul, which has been defiled or afflicted by old age.
The meaning is "for the sake of liberation"; however, that [liberation] is due to being purified by battle, and especially because of being slain by Rāmabhadra.
It is a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) in the form of the edge of a sword, and also one in the form of a stream of water.
It flashes forth;
this is the pure *viṣkambhaka* (interlude),
concerning what has occurred— the slaughter of Kumbhakarṇa and others— and what is about to occur.
And because it indicates the slaying of Rāvaṇa and other events in brief; and its purity arises from being employed by the principal character.
"By means of an aerial vehicle" (*ākāśayānena*) refers to a celestial chariot (*vimāna*).

The entry of the two *vidyādhara*s is for the purpose of describing the battle; this is because such a thing cannot be seen by direct perception. Thus it has been said: "Long journeys, killing, and battle..."
The upheaval of the kingdom, country, and so forth; imprisonment, eating, bathing, sexual union, and anointing with unguents.
"One should not point to perceptible things such as the seizing of clothes" (108).
[The commentary begins with] "Aho," etc.; from *bahoḥ*, meaning from a vast (*vipulāt*) period of time.

The meaning is "after a long time"; here, the word *bahu* denotes abundance, as in the expression "much rice" (*bahurodana*), for if it were intended to signify a number, the plural form would have been used.
The phrase "as if free from fear" (*nirātaṅkamiva*) [is used].

*Ātaṅkaḥ* means fear, [caused] by Rāvaṇa; the word *iva* is a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*), or it indicates that Rāvaṇa’s prowess has become as good as blunted. In the phrase *sañcarāvaha*, the suffix *taṅ* (the *ātmanepada* ending) is applied according to the rule *samastṛtīyāyuktāt* (Pāṇini 1.3.54).
"O Lord of the Gods," and so forth.

"To Indra, they are to be presented" means they are worthy of being offered; that is to say, having offered them to him, they were brought by Rāvaṇa for the purpose of adorning [him]. For this very reason...

"Praise" (ślāghā) refers to the excellence of the prosperity of the welfare of others acquired through valor; "by those superior to that" means by the *toraṇas*, i.e., the outer gateways. That which is praised is "praiseworthy" (*ślāghanī*).

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*) according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam* (Pāṇini 3.3.113). According to Amarasimha, *toraṇa* means "an outer gate" (*bahirdvāra*). She is called a *sakhī* (friend/companion) because she acts as an assistant due to the difficulty of the situation.

"Karṇīrathas" refers to pleasure-cars. Regarding the statement that "in which [city] the streets on all sides were crowded with pleasure-cars filled with women eager to witness the battle"—why say this? For even in the sky, the inhabitants of celestial chariots (*vaimānikas*) find no room.
Thus [ends the twenty-third].
"Etā" and so forth. *Palam* means flesh;
one who eats (*atti*) it is a *palāda*, namely Rāvaṇa, according to the rule "the suffix *aṇ* is added after a verbal root when an object is present" (Pāṇini 3.2.1).
*Sautrāmaṇīnām* refers to those [oblations] dedicated to Indra (*aindrī*). *Asrāmbhaḥ* [means blood-water].

Because they are bound; "deva" means cloud, and those whose mother is the nourisher (mātṛ) are "others than that," meaning "river-nourished" (nadīmātṛka); [this is derived] by the rule *nadyṛtaśca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153), which prescribes the suffix *kap*.
The meaning is that the growth of the groves occurs solely through the streams of tears shed by Indra while imprisoned.
In every birth— birth after birth— he was [harassed] by children, that is,
by cavillers (*vaitaṇḍika*) who delight solely in refuting the prowess of others while being devoid of establishing their own position.

One who merely refutes the position of others is a *vaitaṇḍika*; [the term] *vaitaṇḍika* means one who is skilled (*sādhu*) in *vitaṇḍā* (cavil); [the suffix] *-ṭhak* is applied after words such as *kathā*.
For this very reason, having concealed Rāvaṇa’s defeat at the hands of Arjuna and others,
[the poets] have made even children mockers of Indra’s sole victory and defeat, [claiming] that children too can overcome Indra.
"Thus" is an expression of excessive pride on the part of the citizens. //24//

"Rākṣasas," and so forth. We hear that Vṛtra and others existed even in former times; [the ātmanepada ending] *taṅ* is applied by the rule "samo gamyṛcchi" (Pāṇini 1.3.29). He remains awake (*jāgartti*).
*sma-ajāgaḥ*; by the rule *laṭ sme* (Pāṇini 3.2.119), the present tense suffix (*laṭ*) is used for the past.
*Vipad-viṣaye 'laṅkarmīṇaḥ* means "capable of producing an action in the form of calamity"; this is in the sense of *alaṃ karmaṇaḥ*, according to the rule *paryādayo glānādy-arthe* (Pāṇini 2.2.18).
Thus is the compound; by the rule beginning with "aṣaḍakṣa" (Pāṇini 5.4.107), the suffix *kha* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*).
He whose doorkeeper is Sahasrākṣa himself.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "At his command, he acts like a pillar; what is that Rāvaṇa like?"—that is to say, who is he?
He stands at the gate because he is unfit for entry; the sense is that since Indra has been defeated, the three worlds protected by him are likewise defeated. //25//
*Pratolī* means a street or thoroughfare. When it is being given or struck, it refers to the drum (*paṭaha*) for the purpose of equipping the soldiers.
Regarding the phrase "dig-dantāvala," and so forth: *danta* (ivory) and *mauktika* (pearls) were used in abundance for the purpose of pillars and garlands.
In which archways [these] were displayed;
for such is the dual nature of an archway. And they possessed such archways and were adorned with garlands.
"From *asman*, *yusmad*, *medha*, and *sraj*, [the suffix] *viniḥ* [is applied].
(122) "Accepted" means "consented to. It is said that the master has been bound in chains; what indeed [can be done]?
"We are her attendants"—thus she abandoned the sorrow of being taken captive by the immortals.
She was a friend through the very act of playing in the dust; for children indeed [play] with dust.

Having played together, they become affectionate toward one another; the meaning is that from the time Rāvaṇa took possession [of them], there has been no defeat of Laṅkā. By reason of their kinship, they are *śauṇḍīrāḥ*—that is, arrogant.
For those connected to queens become arrogant because they are exempt from punishment.
By them, "surabhayaḥ" means those who are objects of respect; for it is said that "saurabhya is the weightiness of one's virtues."
Keśava:
(125) They are agitated, shattered, or become bewildered; the sense is that this occurs due to the confusion caused by the armor of the Rākṣasas and the resonance of the sound of the drums.
"According to Amarasimha, the word *gṛha* is used in the masculine and only in the plural sense. (126) //26//
"Having heard," and so forth.
A forest fire becomes a burner only when dependent upon the wind,
but as for the fire named Rāma—
The sense is that in the burning of the Rākṣasa forest, he requires only his own internal equipment (sāmagrī),
and not external things such as chariots, armor, or weapons. And regarding the matter of his defeat,
"running" means going— namely, fleeing.
"Fallen into the interval" means, in the context of victory and defeat, being neutral;
"mugdhā" means deluded, in one sense.
Because of proclaiming one's own defeat. //27//
Compassion arises from seeing those who suffer.
"O Wise One," and so forth; because it was established by Brahmā, even its name [is significant].
The phrase "it is taught" (*śiṣṭam*) is a stylistic turn of expression. "Acting contrarily" (*viceṣṭamānām*) means acting in opposition.
"To revile" (*adhikṣeptum*) means to censure. The word "thus" (*evam*) refers back to the meaning of the preceding verse. [They are] not [the ones who are] suffering.
The sense is that [the act] is censurable.
Regarding the passage beginning with "hastam" (the hand): it means in a place not far to the right of the hand; [this construction is justified by the rule] "enapā dvitīyā" (Pāṇini 2.3.31).
"Mahājanaḥ" means a multitude. "Nyañcat" and so forth:
it refers to extreme bending due to the weight of the feet, with the intended meaning being the *candrahāsa* sword.
"Vyāpṛtā" means arms eager to seize simultaneously;
"by them, the circle of the quarters was pervaded.
"Pratyanīkam" means toward the enemy; "in the prasara," that is, in the movement [of attack].
*sarabhasaḥ* means "with joy"; according to Amarasimha, *rabhasaḥ* [denotes] both speed and joy.
(128) *nirjihīte* means "he goes out. //28//

*Dṛṣṭacara* means previously seen; [the suffix] *caraṭ* is applied in the sense of "having occurred before" (Pāṇini 5.3.53). *Sāṃgrāmika* means arising from battle (*saṅgrāma*), [formed] by virtue of belonging to the *adhyātmādi* group.
The suffix *ṭhañ* (130): *ojāyitam* means acting like *ojas* (vital energy); the sense is that it causes distress to others. [This is formed by] the suffix *kyaṅ* after a word denoting the agent.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied by the rule *salopaśca* (Pāṇini 3.1.13); from that, the past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*) is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*).
*Ayātayāma* means "fresh"; Amarasimha states: "*yātayāma* is that whose essence has departed."

*bhīṣayate* means "it causes fear" or "it produces terror"; [the suffix] *taṅ* (ātmanepada) is applied by the rule *bhīsmyorhetubhaye* (Pāṇini 1.3.68), which states that [the ātmanepada suffix is used after the roots *bhī* and *smi* when the cause of fear is expressed].
*Bhiyo hetubhaye*.
He says that very thing in the verse beginning with "marutvaddambholi" (the thunderbolt of Indra):
even for a moment at the fall of the thunderbolt.
*Śvayathuḥ* means swelling (*śothaḥ*); this is a statement regarding the firmness of his limbs. *Āpītam* means pervaded (*vyāptam*); the meaning is that he has a broad chest (*viśālavakṣas*).
*Devadrīcīm* means going toward the gods (*devagāminīm*); [this is according to] *Pāṇini 5.2.136*: *viṣvag-devayoḥ*.
By such [rules] as these,
there is the substitution of *adri*; "one who goes toward the gods is *devadryaṅ*," according to Amara.

Bringing the goddess Śrī under the control of his own arm, he spoke these words: "The Goddess of Fortune remains here like a female elephant in the forest. The sense is that when the thunderbolt was rendered useless, sovereign rule was recovered from Indra who had been conquered. At that time, how did it come to be? Her—
"Indeed, do you remember the form?"—by this statement of having been seen previously, there is a recollection of its having undergone change over time. //29//
"Enam" and so forth.
*Vyāja* means deceit (*kapaṭa*); as Amara states: "Deceit is *vyāja*, not feminine.
The meaning is that they are "blameless" because they are brought about by unrestrained intentions. For this very reason, the word *kalpataru* (wish-fulfilling tree) is employed.
"He propitiates" means he pleases. By this, the "alliance of tribute" (*upahārasandhi*) is described.

Regarding this, Kāmandaka says: "That which arises from a gift is called an *upahāra* (tribute)" (139). "What more [need be said]?"—even Indra, the lord of the celestial wish-fulfilling trees, is in such a state; how much more so one who is merely a god, by virtue of being subject to perpetual tribute?

And because it is empty-handed, the ocean is "miserable" (dīna), so to speak; [this refers to] the fear of being struck by a punishment even greater than that constant penalty which is fixed even for an offense. As for the possibility of such an excess of punishment:

Regarding the phrase "even those to be carried by the [other] aggregates": because he had previously promised that he would give even those things to be carried by the aggregates when fewer were brought than what could be carried by the human aggregates.
However, the meaning is that he had previously given those things to be carried by camels, carts, and so forth. *Apadiśan* means "in order to give";
the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used here in the sense of cause (*hetau*). (140) "Even in the act of giving, there may be an *apadeśa* (pretext); it may also mean 'telling'."
"Cāpadeśanam" means "a pretext," according to Keśava.
(141) "Devoid of wealth" refers to mines whose essence has been extracted through daily extraction; [he entered them] somehow or other.
"Parishodhayati" means he investigates; the sense is that [the enemy] lacks an abundance of superior [resources].
Alternatively, "skandhopaneyāt" means because of a specific type of treaty (*sandhi-viśeṣa*); regarding this, Kāmandaka says:
"That [treaty] where a fixed amount of wealth is given for each *skandha* (division of the army) is called 'skandhopaneya'."

"People who understand the meaning [of a treaty] call it *sandhi*. (142) The meaning of this is as follows: *paricchinna* means determined that "I shall give this at such a time"; *skandha* is the name...
A mutual agreement made regarding the time limit for the payment of wealth;
[this refers to] one who, out of fear of incurring a heavier penalty for failing to pay the promised wealth,
tells him that his own mines are devoid of jewel-treasures— [this is an example of] "the mention of an action" (*kriyāgrahaṇam*).
The fourth [line] is "kartavyam" (143). By this, it is meant:
"One should explain the exhaustion of karmas while speaking of the goal" (144).
The exhaustion of karma as stated by Kauṭilya has been mentioned;
its meaning is as follows— according to the second position:

When his ascetic practice has become fruitless, he "purifies his purpose"— that is, through the repayment of the promised jewels from his debts— he purifies himself by means of the performance of actions such as agriculture and trade, which are the causes for the acquisition of wealth.
The meaning is that for one who has made such a vow, there is purity in that giving. //30//
*Parāpatitaḥ* means arrived. *Vanāyu* is the name of the birthplace of the best horses;
regarding these superior horses, it has been said: "The *vanāyuja*, *phārasīka*, *kāmboja*, and *bāhlīka* horses [are the best]. (145)
The Kīnāśakāsāra is the buffalo that serves as Yama’s vehicle (146); it causes a fever in his ears because of its innate enmity. As it has been said: "The cow-tiger..."
"Elephant, lion, horse, and buffalo"—
this is the context regarding natural enemies.
"At the end of the eon," and so forth.
*Sūrāḥ* means suns. *Vikaṭāni* means terrifying.
*Kaṇḍūyantaḥ* means itchy; [from the rule] "from *kaṇḍū* and others... [the suffix *śatṛ* is applied].
Because of the elision of *yak* (by Pāṇini 3.1.67), it is a verb that takes both voices (*ubhayapadī*). *Ūrjasvalāḥ* means "possessing strength" or "powerful";
[the suffix *-vala-*] is a *nipāta* by the rule beginning with *jyotsnātamisrā* (Pāṇini 5.2.114).
*Vilakṣaḥ*: ashamed because of having twenty arms equipped for hand-to-hand combat with two hands.
*Uttiṣṭhamānāḥ*: striving to fight; [according to Pāṇini 1.3.24] "the prefix *ud-* [is used] when the action is not upward. (151)
Thus [it is said].
(152) *Goṣṭhī* means a gathering. The sense is that, as gold is tested on a touchstone, one's pride in learning (*suramada*) is diminished here. *Kaikaseya* means the son of Kaikeyī.
"Ḍhak after [words ending in] strī" (Pāṇini 4.1.120). He prepares = he makes [to fight] against Rāvaṇa.
It goes out; the meaning is that the two forces assemble for battle. //31//

He says that very thing: "Agastya," and so forth. There is a story that in ancient times Agastya held back the Vindhya mountain—which was growing out of envy toward Mount Meru and obstructing the path of the sun—and thus shattered it. For this very reason, [the mountains] were "deficient" due to their lack of height.
"Uneven" means unsuitable for the construction of stone embankments; therefore, they are not attached to the bridge, meaning they have been discarded.
Stones unfit for binding will be cast away;
[the monkeys] were lifting them up for the purpose of battle.

Because the word *śikhara* belongs to the *ardharca*-class (Pāṇini 2.4.31), it optionally takes the masculine gender; furthermore, there is a grammatical rule for both masculine and neuter genders stating: "The gateways have thousands of pillars and coals as their peaks" (*andhakāraśikharasahasrāṅgāratoraṇāḥ*). In this interval, [he] arrived.
Having seen the ten-headed man and determined him to be Rāvaṇa,
[he acted] out of a desire to see him more specifically.
The meaning is that having approached nearby, they fled quickly out of fear;
"satyāpitaḥ" means ascertained.
By the rule "satyāpapāśa" (Pāṇini 3.1.25), the causative suffix *ṇic* is applied;
by the rule "arthavedasatyānām kṛtau" (Pāṇini 3.1.25),
the augment *āpuk* is added in conjunction with that suffix.
*Capalam* means quickly; as Amarasimha states: "Quickly, swiftly, rapidly" (159). //32//
"Made into weapons," and so forth. *Palam* means meat.

(160) *Utkramya* means having leaped up. He says "rejoices" to indicate fearlessness; for since meat is a heavy food, it causes burning sensations, and thus [he rejoices] in the absence of such [consequences] for its eater.
The term "candāla" (outcaste) is used because of their dependence on [the killing of] sandalwood.
"Dadhate" means they take hold of;
[the phrase "pāśabandhaduḥkhavāsikām"] means [they dwell in suffering] as if by means of bonds and fetters.

The sense is that [the suffix] *ṇvul* is used in the instruction on the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) to denote "staying" (*sthiti*), and not to denote the "affliction by poison" (*viṣabādha*). For this very reason, there is the statement "in the parts" (*avayaveṣu*), and not otherwise.
The meaning is: "in the bodily constituents such as the rasa. Serpents [render their venom] ineffective because it is applied for the purpose of harming enemies who reside within their own bodies.
The meaning of the word "tu" (but) is that she performs that task herself. Regarding the word "kṣaṇa":
the sense is that at another moment, having released them, she moves them away. //33//
"Protect," and so forth.

*Viḍamba* means imitation. Their turning away [from him] is due precisely to his being a *rākṣasa*, since they are celestial nymphs (*suravadhū*). "Struck" means beaten. Nevertheless, the acquisition of flowers occurred.
This is the intended meaning; here, "sleep" refers to death. //34//
"svatanu" and so forth. With the words "ito dyām," he points to the region where he himself is situated;
by this, it is indicated that the direction in which Rāma is situated is "anapāyī" (unfailing), for observers remain in a location that does not shift. "Dīrghāhnīm" means having long days.

"Prakāśavatīm" means "possessing light"; [the feminine suffix] *ṅīp* is applied here according to Pāṇini 4.1.39 (*ana upadhālopino 'nyatarasyām*). "Ābhogaḥ" means "expansion. "Akāṇḍe" means "at an inappropriate time."
Because it is not in one's hand, there is an absence of opportunity; Amara states: "The word *kāṇḍa*—not feminine—is used for a staff, an arrow, a reed, a section, an occasion, and water.
Of him who makes [the night] dark; [from the suffixes] *asmāyāmedhāsrajaḥ*.
"Viniḥ-":
the word "parito dyām" (all around the sky) is to be supplied as the remainder. By the word "ahaḥ" (day), the solar nature of the *haris* is indicated; [this occurs] prior to the battle.
Those Rākṣasas who were astonished by Abhimanyu as if by darkness in the presence of the sun, they themselves [were now amazed] while he fought with them as they blazed with rage.
The meaning is that they perish like smoke when the fire has increased. //35//
"Something" (*kimapi*), etc.:

"something" means that which is impossible to describe. "With trees as weapons" (*tarubhiḥ śastribhiḥ*). "Filling" (*pratibharaṇikā*) means the act of filling; from the root *bhṛ* (in the sense of "supporting" or "nourishing") with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the abstract sense (*bhāve*), and then expressing the feminine gender.

The suffix *ṅīp* [is applied]; according to Amarasimha, "A woman (*strī*) may be something like a lotus stalk (*mṛṇālī*) when there is a desire to express diminution (*apacaya*). Here, *apacaya* refers to femininity; from that, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*).
With the shortening [of the vowel] by the rule *ṅyāpoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.63) and the addition of the suffix *ṭāp*,
the form [is established].
Monkeys perform such a task— that is, they engage in battle.
By such means, those waters in the form of Rāvaṇa’s fame— which previously found no space at all within the quarters filled by the Rākṣasas— [now overflow].

Having spread across the quarters as if they were their natural shores, those very [stars] now occupy the extremities of the directions in order to fill the center of the sky, which has been emptied by the descent of the rākṣasa.
They abandon the center of the western direction— that is to say, they contract—
because when a stone or similar object situated in the middle is removed, the water recedes downward.
Or rather, [it is] by means of the falling rows of *rakṣas* demons, precisely because of their falling.
By the "pratibharaṇikā"—meaning a dam serving as a reservoir—by which the middle of the sky was filled with its own relinquished [water];
here the root *bhṛ* has the sense of supporting or holding. (172)
"Devoid of firmness" means lacking stability; for when a dam is broken, the water recedes from the banks. //36//
"Crushed by the Rakshasa," and so forth. *Nipiṣṭāḥ* means pulverized (*cūrṇitāḥ*).
*Ujjihānaḥ* means appearing (*āvirbhavan*).
*Aṭṭahāsaḥ* means a loud laugh (*atihāsaḥ*).
The manifestation of anger;
as it has been said: "Gazing at one's own arms, roaring from the throat, and so forth, [occur] when there is anger toward an enemy. (173) Thus, there is the roaring from the throat.
Here is a hyperbole: that Rāvaṇa,
with showers of arrows whose interiors were filled with pulverized mountains— like a cloud with torrents whose interiors are filled with spray— [obscured] the sun.
The meaning is that it covers. //37//
"By the base ones," and so forth.
"To render useless" means to afflict. "Not difficult" means easy.
He says that very thing: "The arrogant," and so forth. "Dantāvala" means an elephant; [as stated in the lexicon] "dantaśikhā..."
The suffix *valac* is applied by the rule *saṃjñāyām* (Pāṇini 5.2.137), and the lengthening of the vowel occurs by the rule *anyeṣām api dṛśyate* (Pāṇini 6.3.137).
The meaning is that elephants are terrified by the mere sight [of him].
The word *tārā* is used because it is the cause of *avagraha*, which is the obstruction of rain;
*tārāḥ* refers to the pupils of the eyes, and *tārāḥ* also refers to the planets, such as Mars (*bhauma*) and the others.
By the phrase "stretching out their necks" (*udgrīvayanta*), he expresses agitation; that is what it means.
The suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of "he causes to do"; thus, even Rāvaṇa, the conqueror of the lords of the quarters, was thrown into confusion— this is [the reason for] the monkeys'.
This is a statement regarding the power of every assault. "By the remaining ones" means by those in excess.
"Uddāmānaḥ" means unrestrained. Regarding the word "purīm," the rule "enapā dvitīyā" (Pāṇini 2.3.31) applies.
They float, meaning they rush forth for the sake of battle. //38//
*Kaṇṭakitāḥ* means bristling with horripilation due to the joy of rending the chests of enemies.

*Vīrapāṇam* refers to the drinking of liquor and other such drinks performed at the beginning of a battle and so forth for the sake of increasing intoxication; the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule *vā bhāvakaraṇayoḥ* (Pāṇini 8.4.178).

Regarding the term *vīrapāṇa*, Amarasimha states: "The drinking that occurs when a battle has already taken place or is about to take place is called *vīrapāṇa*. For the purpose of drinking, there is a *goṣṭhī*, which means a social gathering; therein—

"Those for whom great drinking festivals have increased. The word *kṛtam* is an indeclinable used in the sense of prohibition; Vardhamāna states: "The word *kṛtam* is used in the senses of warding off and negation. (180) The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) with *viṣādena*; thus, it refers to wretched speech caused by despondency. Since there was no defeat of the monkeys—which would have been the cause of such [speech]—do not... [speak]. (181)
The sense is "let it be so.
Regarding the passage beginning with "O ten-faced one" (*daśamukha*):
*paripucchayamānāḥ* means having their tails whirled about during flight.

This is the nature of monkeys: the suffix *ṇiṅ* is used in the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) in the expression "one who fights with his tail as his only vessel" (*pucchabhāṇḍa*), etc.; he fights facing toward the enemy.
The words "together with himself" (*ātmanā saha*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis; the *parasmaipada* ending is used according to the rule beginning with *budhayudha* (Pāṇini 1.3.96). //39//
"Filled with sorrow," and so forth:
sorrow arises from the fruitlessness of Sugrīva's efforts; laughter arises because that which came as a destroyer has itself perished; and wonder arises from reflecting upon the power of Rāvaṇa.
The sound "ahaha" is that which manifests the three aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
Regarding the phrase "the missiles" and so forth:
they are "ordained as missiles," meaning they have been employed as such.
Those burnt by the fire born of their own conflict perish. //40//
"This is nothing at all"— the sense is that for one who has uprooted Kailāsa, the mere pulverization of a mountain is not difficult.
He says that very thing with the words "tathā" and so forth. *Sphaṭikaśikharī* is Kailāsa.
The particle *api* is used in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). *Uddhṛtya* means having uprooted.
*Truṭitena* means by what was severed; [specifically] by the support of the earth. Likewise, [the rest follows].
"Vidhuraḥ" means rendered supportless; "yena" refers to that distress caused by the loss of the kinsman of the earth.
"Vyatikaraḥ" means contact; [here it refers to] the commencement of the dance.
This means: "of the peaks," in front—that is, at the forefront—it "undulates," meaning it moves;
the sense is that this [wind] alone moves among other mountains, for it is indeed unsupported that moves. Or alternatively: "of the peaks."
When there is a desire to express mere relationship, the ablative case does not occur; the meaning is: "First he moves, afterwards others move. (41)
Regarding the phrase "made into a weapon" and so forth: although the great tree was employed as a weapon by the powerful [Hanumān], its falling gently was due to the extreme strength of Rāvaṇa.

Regarding "ājaghāna": the absence of the middle voice (ātmanepada) is due to the rule *āṅo yamahanaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.28), because the object is external to the agent (*parāṅgakarmakatvāt*). The sense is that even though the flowers were rendered fruitless for their own support, [the tree] did not itself perform what ought to have been done for them.
This statement is made because flowers are indeed stimulants. //42//
"What is being said? means it is impossible to say; the ellipsis is "its existence. Regarding the phrase "Rāvaṇa indeed":
the sense is that even in the absence of a specific description, his existence is recognized by people merely by hearing his name.

He speaks precisely of the state of being a *mahāsattva*: "In their own," and so forth. "Alike" (*alikeṣu*) means on the bones of the forehead. "Having burst open" (*sphuṭitvā*) means having split apart.
"By means of scripts" (*lipibhiḥ*) means by those inscribed upon the forehead. "The *Rāmāyaṇa*" refers to the life-story of Rāma;
that is to say, the account of Rāma’s self-slaughter. [This is derived from] "from a preceding word... [referring to the rule governing the formation of the compound].

The substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] occurs by the rule "saṃjñāyāmagaḥ" (Pāṇini 8.4.3). By this [verse], which is intent upon the composition as a whole, the subject matter—killing—is indicated. Here, Skanda says: "Life-span, action, wealth, knowledge, and death—these five..."
"The [karmic marks] are engraved even upon the embodied being while still in the womb" (190).
"Even having seen"— that is, even having ascertained— "more than that" means [the suffering] arising from the severing of the head.

A satisfaction greater than [ordinary] satisfaction, because his mind does not falter even when certain of his own death; for this very reason, there is honor. "To him" (*tasmai*): the status of the recipient (*sampradāna*) is established by the rule *krudhadruha-* (Pāṇini 1.4.37). *Vairāyate* means he creates enmity.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied [after a word] beginning with "śabdavaira" (192), etc. //43//

It was terrifying due to the possibility of Sugrīva’s defeat; it was wonderful upon considering the two forces. He expresses this very point with the words beginning "viśikha" (arrows) and so forth: "in the tumultuous," that is, in the chaotic battle; "tumulam."
"Raṇasaṅkula" means a tumultuous battle (Amara-kośa 1.8.10). "Gaṇḍaśailāḥ" refers to large boulders fallen from a mountain (Amara-kośa 2.3.6).
"Talātaliprapañcāḥ" refers to the various expansions of wrestling; [it is so called] because of striking with both palms used as weapons.

The battle proceeded as *talātali*; [this is formed] by the *bahuvrīhi* compound according to Pāṇini 2.2.27 (*tatra tenedam iti sarūpe*), with the suffix *ic* added according to Pāṇini 5.4.127 (*ic karmavyatihāre*).

The vowel lengthening occurs by the rule "anyeṣām api dṛśyate" (Pāṇini 6.3.137); because it ends in *ij*, it is designated as an indeclinable (*avyaya*) due to its inclusion in the *tiṣṭhadgu* group and its status as an *avyayībhāva* compound. //44//
"Wave of breath," and so forth. "Wave" (*ūrmi*) means a succession;

"obstruction" (*pratibandha*) means cessation, because the channels are stiffened by the earth due to its excessive weight from being stepped upon by Sugrīva. For this very reason, there is thickness of the throat.
The breaking of the necklace;
by those falling—that is, having fallen—with the suffix *āluc* according to the rule "spṛhigṛhi" (Pāṇini 3.2.158);
*prāgbhāra* means a mass. By the sound of the falling jewels.
The delusion that the bones of the hoods were broken arose from their mutual contact; they were rigid, meaning firm. *Vikrama* refers to the movement of the feet. //45//
He replies to [the opponent] who is motionless due to being crushed by the arm-machine with the words beginning with "asmad" (our):
*āndola* means swinging; by that, the fruit is easily obtained.
The form of remaining at ease; in wrestling—that is, in arm-to-arm combat—lightness means agility. It is desired that one who is fatigued should find rest;
and the meaning is that this has been accomplished by you, O monkey, through the swinging of our forest-like arms.
*Śākhāmṛgaḥ* means a monkey;
according to Amarasimha, "kapi, plavaṅga, plavaga, and śākhāmṛga" [are synonyms]. [He is mentioned] because he is a source of joy for the forest, and also for the sake of humiliation.
The statement regarding his being a "branch-monkey" (śākhāmṛga). //46//

*Karaṇāni* refers to specific actions such as those of the arms and so forth; by means of skill (*kauśalena*) in these. [As it is said: "The word *karaṇa* is used in the senses of an instrument, a field, a task, a secretary, and action."
"Even in the case of songs, bodily movements, postures, actions, distinctions, and the senses," so says the *Viśvaprakāśa*.
(201) *Hṛdayaṅgamam* means "consonant with the heart," that is to say, "consistent with reason"; [the word] *saṅgatam*...
"Heart-captivating" (hṛdayaṅgama), according to Amara.
Regarding "by twenty," and so forth:
in the propitiation of Maheśvara, there is attraction with ten [recitations] and cutting with ten.
Even while you were enduring, the tenth head was severed;
your heads, for which the order of their severance had been indicated, were cut off all at once, simultaneously.
"Having cut [it] with just ten claws"—the meaning is: "then may I, the lord of the forest-dwellers, be at ease.
The passage beginning with "ārāddha" (propitiated) indicates invincibility.

From this point up to the end of the verse, "Our chariots cry out" (203), because it consists of the humiliation of Rāvaṇa, it is the dramatic element named *chalana* (deception); as it has been said: "Deception, however, is humiliation" (204).
Thus //47//
"Ten-faced," and so forth.

"Slaughter itself" refers to *nāṭya*, that is, a dramatic work (*rūpaka*), because it is the cause of joy for the audience who possess the forms of deities; of that [drama], the *sūtradhāra* is the director of the performers.
Pāripārśvika: One who acts by leaving the side— that is, moving away from the side— and who, as such, is the actor (abhinetā) who prompts another character toward the director (sūtradhāra).
Because, having departed from its side and abandoned it, one subsequently enters [it] again; therefore, it is "pari" in this context.

It has the sense of "avoiding" (or "excluding"). As Bharata states: "When the Sūtradhāra has exited along with his followers, one should then expand upon the subject matter (*vastu*) through the characters (*pātra*) introduced by him. (205–206)

*Anugaḥ* means *pāripārśvikaḥ* (an attendant). In the rule *parimukhaṃ ca* (Pāṇini 5.1.12), by virtue of the word *ca*, the suffix *ṭhak* is applied after the word *paripārśva* when it is in the second case and denotes the sense of "being present" (*vartamāna-arthe*).
The suffix *ṭhak* occurs after a word ending in *vahati* (Pāṇini 4.4.76);
even though the root *vṛt* is intransitive, this [suffix] takes a word in the second case as its governing object.

Because it possesses a form that is to be accomplished (*niṣpādyatva*), it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the meaning expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) which has attained the status of an object (*karmatva*); for instance, in the case of *śobhanaṃ vartate*, the meaning is "he performs a beautiful act of being" (*śobhanaṃ vartanaṃ karoti*).

This has been stated: "It should be stated that adverbs (kriyāviśeṣaṇa) have the status of an object (karman) and are neuter. Regarding this, the *Kāśikā* says: "An adverb functions like an object even for verbs that do not otherwise take an object. [This applies to] Rāma’s...
The state of being the *sūtradhāra* (stage-manager) arises from his role as the instigator; his own status as the *pāripārśvika* (assistant) follows by his command.
Because it initiates the battle with Rāvaṇa, that which is "practiced" or "imitated"— namely, the conduct of the actions prescribed by the three Vedas— is the *prakaraṇa* (drama); therein,
the "fruit" (*phala*) is the fifth [element], consisting of the commencement, effort, and so forth, to be accomplished.

The seed (*bīja*) is that which is to be tasted through the nature of the matter (*arthaprakṛti*); by means of those two—the *nirvahaṇa* and the *mukha*, which characterize the junctures (*sandhi*)—the three intermediate junctures are implied according to the principle of ellipsis (*pratyāhāra*). (212)
The "cultivators" (*bhāvakāḥ*) of those junctures (*sandhi*) are those who contemplate the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors residing therein; for this very reason,
they are "consumers of nectar" (*amṛtabhujaḥ*).
And they are the experiencers of the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), such as the unsurpassed bliss of the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
By the word "assembly" (*samāja*), it is indicated that these very people are the spectators (*sāmājika*).
Thus, "we worship together."
"Supreme for one's own group" means: "I shall gladden Indra and the other gods by slaying you. //48//

Regarding the passage beginning with *yanmālya*: for that head of Rāvaṇa (*yasmai rāvaṇamūrdhne*), [the garland] is suitable; this is a compound with the middle term elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ*); because there is no relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛtivikārābhāvāt*), it is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
The prohibition of the fourth-case compound (*caturthī-samāsa*). *Mālya* is that which is to be placed upon the hair;
as Amarasimha states: "The words *mālya*, *mālā*, and *sraj* refer to a garland on the head" (2.6.105). Because of its being woven, [the flowers] remain...
Thus—"the remaining ones," [formed] with the suffix *ac* after the root *pac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134); "by those"; because they are "defective" (*vikalāni*), i.e., damaged by insects and the like;
[it is] by such *santāna* flowers, acting as causes.
"Secretly" means hidden out of fear of Rāvaṇa; "by those who were garland-makers.
"Only a small amount" means it was to be placed within the hair itself—that is, very little; [the phrase] "in the midst of the hair" refers to...
According to Amara, *garbhaka* means "interior" or "womb"; *gumphita* means "strung together" or "knotted.

The statement regarding Rāvaṇa’s prowess—that "even for the Lord of Gods this state [of being bound] has occurred"—indicates that the very striking of his head was the resulting calamity (*prastāvanā*), meaning its attainment.
*Rabhasaḥ* means joy. (218) *Syandanāḥ* refers to those situated there [on the chariots] by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇayā*);
they "cry out," meaning they raise a great clamor. //49//
"Of the expansion," and so forth.
Expansion (*prathana*) means battle (*yuddha*). In that regard, there are first victory and defeat.
The sense is that these two do not bring about excellence; rather, it is only the last two that do so.
Regarding the passage beginning with "son of Kuśika" and ending with "service": for knowledge acquired through service leads to its fruition.
