*Sahayudhvā* means "one who has fought together"; by the rule *sahe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.96) within the section on primary suffixes (*bhūtādhikāra*), the suffix *kvanip* is applied to the root *yudh*. For this very reason, *vīrabhoga* means "battle."
"Taddhitabāhuḥ" (having arms [strengthened] by secondary suffixes); the suffix *kha* is applied according to the rule "ātmanviśvajana" (Pāṇini 4.2.42).
By this, he states the collection of factors for victory. With the word "kautuka," he expresses the enthusiasm that is the root of victory. //50//
"By a fool as well," and so forth.
The particle *api* expresses possibility. "Causing to sweat" (*svedayatā*) means making [someone] possess sweat (*svedavantam*);
the suffix *matup* is applied to the word *sveda* in the sense of possession.
By the rules "arśa-ādibhyo 'c" (Pāṇini 5.2.127) and "tat karoti" (Pāṇini 3.1.26), the suffix Ṇic is applied.

The suffix *śatṛ* [indicates the present tense]. *Ūṣman* means strength and heat. Just as bamboo and other materials are straightened by the heat of steam, so too was the haughty Bhārgava calmed through his majesty (*pratāpa*).

The meaning is "he has done. There is a lengthening [of the vowel] by the rule *cvau ca* (Pāṇini 7.4.26). By the force of the principle that "it is action alone that implies an agent, not a substance," the word *vālin* denotes a substance.

One intent on the act of killing: "The killing of you, who are inferior to Vālin, is appropriate even by one inferior to Rāma; thus, even so, there is an excess of praise in saying 'he killed him who had already killed Vālin.'"

He shall attain [this]; therefore, you are fortunate. What more is there to say? The meaning is that there is no gain whatsoever superior to equality with one’s own conqueror. In other words, today you shall be slain by Rāma. //51//
Regarding the passage beginning with "yatkanyām" (when [he asked] for the girl): *nimipati* is Janaka.
*Tulitāvatāritaḥ* means lifted up and then set down; it is a worldly convention that one who can lift and set down a great weight by himself is possessed of great strength.
The fact that the divine bow was not broken, even though the desire for fruit and strength were present, is what is meant by "not breaking";
this is used figuratively.

The infamy rooted in that consists of public rumor in the form of the saying: "He did not break it because he was incapable, despite its strength being even greater than that of Kailāsa. The fact that the bow possesses a power exceeding that of the world is stated in the verse beginning with "worshipped by the Lord of Mountains" (2.29).
That is infamy,
the karma [resulting] from the cruel energy of obstructing the rain of the noble elephant Airāvata; thus it is called "splitting."

"From roots ending in *ṣit* and from *bhidādi* etc., the suffix *aṅ* [is applied]. (Pāṇini 3.3.104). "As far as you... (*yāvad bhavān*). Here, the word *yāvat* is used in the sense of a temporal limit, meaning "at what time will you arrive? Regarding the rule "both *yāvat* and *tāvat* [are used] in the senses of totality and limit": [the former denotes totality, while the latter denotes a limit].
According to Amara, "māne" means "in restriction" (avadhāraṇe). The ellipsis is "they did not protect [me] for so long.
"Now" means "even though you have arrived. To what extent [of time]?

"Rakṣanti" means "they will protect" (pālayiṣyanti); it means they will not protect. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here because of its proximity to the present time (*vartamānasāmīpye*). The accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoḥ*. Alternatively, [the phrase] is "bhavān adhunā" (you now).
"You were born as one connected to this time"; "until what limit from now on" means "they will protect you"; [this refers to the rule] *yāvat-purā* (Pāṇini 3.3.4).

By the phrase beginning with "ityādinā," the *laṭ* (present tense) suffix is used [to indicate future action]. In the reading "drakṣyanti" (they will see), the words "yat" and "tat" refer to the cause; for even though there was both a desire for the fruit and strength, by that cause—namely, devotion to his master—the bow was not broken; for if the bow had been broken, it would have constituted treachery toward the master.
The meaning is "it might be so. By that very same cause of your death;
even though one who betrays his master ought to be slain, my arrows have conquered Indra, yet you—
"Yāvat" means "to what extent is its measure?"— that is to say, it is very small. Here, although it refers to a measure (*parimāṇa*), [it functions as an adverb].
The word "yāvat" (as far as) functions here in the sense of a limit; therefore, they have disregarded [this matter] for such a long time. "Now," [he says].

"To what extent will they behold you— who have committed the offense of breaking the master’s bow, and who have carried out a succession of offenses such as the assault upon me and the slaying of Kumbhakarna and others?"—
by means of your voice; beyond this point...
The meaning is that they will surely destroy [it]. On this point, Māgha says:
"A forgiving person may well tolerate one who offends slightly or even occasionally; but [he cannot tolerate] one who offends through repeated action."
"Who could endure [this]?
(235). From this point until "he fell at the very feet of Śambhu" (236), this is *vyavasāya* (perseverance/resolution), because it consists of an expression of his own capability.
This is the constituent element of *nāma* (name); as it has been said:
"The expression of one's own power is *vyavasāya*. Here, the word "one's own" (*sva*) is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). //52//

"How even now? means: "even though Rāma, the slayer of his own conquering Vālin, has arrived. The construction is: "the knot in the form of egoism—that very same [knot]; it remains exactly as much as it was."

It is as if connected with a state of well-being; the meaning is that it does not diminish at all. Regarding the form *vismāpayate*: the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied by the rule *bhīsmyorhetubhaye* (Pāṇini 1.3.68), and the substitution of *ā* for *i* is applied by the rule *nityaṃ smayateḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.57).
Even for one who conceives pride (*abhimāna*) toward the Mother of the World, there is a corresponding pride toward her adversary.
He says it is not for the sake of wonder: "puffed up with pride," and so forth.
"Puffed up with pride" means filled with arrogance. "It remains" means it is the remainder (*śeṣa*).
By the rule *pacādyac* (Pāṇini 3.1.134), the suffix *ac* is applied.
Since that [suffix] is one and it is also the remainder (*śeṣa*), a compound is formed according to the rule *pūrvakāla-* (Pāṇini 2.1.49) and so forth. [The word] *strīm* [is thus derived].
By the rule "vāmśasoḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.80), there is an optional substitution of *iyaṅ*.
In his prostration at the feet of Ardhanārīśvara, he cut off nine heads to deceive the Goddess's feet, leaving himself with only one head.

The sense is that, given the abundance of heads, it was even possible for him to touch her with his left foot; for this very reason he was pleased, as he had deceived the Goddess, and so he fell at the feet of Śambhu alone. //53//
"Of the Lord of Heaven," and so forth. The word *iva* is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*).
*Upatiṣṭhate* means "he attains"; the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied according to the rule "after *upa*, [the verb takes the ātmanepada] when meaning worship of a deity" (Pāṇini 1.3.25).
"Do you not see?"—the word "Mātali" is to be supplied as the object.
The sense is that because it is presided over by Indra’s charioteer, it is known as "belonging to Indra" (aindra).
"Candrakāḥ" refers to holes shaped like the moon; by means of these, it is "stabakitaḥ," meaning it appears as if a cluster of flowers has formed there.
The suffix *itac* is applied according to the rule for words beginning with *tāraka* (Pāṇini 5.2.36).
Regarding the phrase "of various kinds" (*vividha*) and so forth:
there is a similarity because the rainbow (*suracāpa*) also possesses various manifestations. By the word *vimāna*,...
A chariot is perceived [there], because it is a vehicle that travels through the sky. "In the midst of battle" means at the time of combat.
"He caused [him] to take up" was done by Mātali. "The bow as well"—the meaning is that it was not merely the armor. Far away...
The meaning is that while it was known only as a "jewel-bow," upon its manifestation, it was known in its true nature as simply a "bow. //54//
*Are re* is used for addressing those of low status.
*Darpo'yam* and so forth. *Doḥkāṇḍāḥ* means *dordaṇḍāḥ* (staff-like arms);
according to Amarasimha, "the word *kāṇḍa* is not feminine and means 'staff' (*daṇḍa*). (Amara-kosa 2.8.96).
Itching is the desire to fight (yuyutsā); that itself is the poison, because it causes a burning sensation. Its flame is [the resulting pain];
the "snake-charmer" (jāṅgulika) for that is the physician of poisons, one who destroys it—meaning, one who conquers the entire world.
"Viṣavaidyaḥ jāṅgulikaḥ" (247) [means] "one who treats with poison" according to Amara;
*jāṅgala* is a specific kind of meat (248). "This one" (*ayam*) means, that is to say, the cause for the desire to seize the adversary. *Api* is used in the sense of a question. By which...

"By means of pride" (*darpeṇa*) refers to the cause. "Of the child" (*śiśoḥ*) indicates a lack of capability to carry out [the task]. This refers to the act of sending him with armor and other equipment. "Dviṣṭam" means hatred; the suffix *niṣṭhā* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). "He will exist" (*vartiṣyate*) means he will live.
According to Amarasimha, "vṛttiḥ vartanajīvane" (vṛtti means livelihood or subsistence).
This [element] is called *dyuti* (splendor), as its nature consists of threatening and terrifying.
As it has been said: "The radiance [of the fire] serves for threatening and terrifying. (251) //55//

"This" refers to the statement of political ethics (*nītivākya*); it is true. To the question "What is that?", he says: "He who is of such character," and so forth. "He" refers to the king, by virtue of the context (252). "These" refers primarily to the attendants;
the meaning is that they are ill-behaved because they have been permeated by the master's misconduct.
The boy was impulsive;
"with anger," and so forth,
[referring to] at the commencement of the battle.
Scorched by anger; and immediately thereafter,
by those [arrows] produced from the sight of his hands—
being "klībaiḥ" means difficult— to endure, even though their arms had already conquered the senses.

The sense is: "Even if there is ill-discipline [on my part], what loss do I suffer because of you? The suffix *ṇini* in the word *vijayin* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlye*). //56//
He spoke with derision: "Having cut," and so forth.
"Vṛtaḥ" means requested; "the glory of victory" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"Vāstavī" means natural; by this, he refers to her habitual character.

The sense is that a request for an object already established by one's own power is futile. It is transitive (dvikarmaka) because it possesses the same meaning as the root *yāc* (to beg). Or rather (*vā*):
since he is the grandson of Brahmā, heads certainly exist [for him], and therefore they are not difficult to obtain; for he is capable of creating the entire world.

The implication is: "Would he be blunted in the fashioning of his own grandson's head? This is a jest, suggesting that [the trees] were cut down because they were easily accessible, and not out of recklessness. //57//

"Are, re"— these are used in contempt arising from anger; "ḍimbha," meaning "child," from this point until the end of "(256) 'Therefore, you do not exist,'" constitutes a speech characterized by rage.
*Saṃpheṭa* is a dramatic element (aṅga);
it is stated as follows: "Saṃpheṭa is speech uttered in anger. (257)
There was a king of the Ikṣvāku lineage named Anaraṇya. (258) The meaning is: "I have killed him who was known as 'the one possessing great knowledge'."
"O son of a Rākṣasī!"—the meaning is that your valor belongs only to your mother and not to your father, whereas mine is not so.
"I am not grieved," and so forth: "I am not grieved" means that I have no sorrow on account of his death, because he was undefeated.

And that [is so] because of the absence of fear from death; however, that which you said— "at the time of the *vāliharaṇa* (the offering of rice-grains), I entreated you for alms"— that causes me distress.
The sense is: "I am distressed because you, who have conquered Arjuna—who himself defeated Bhārgava—have come to fight with me. //58//
“O Kṣatriya,” and so forth.
*Vācāṭa* means one who speaks much that is censurable; according to [Amara-kośa 3.1.46], “*vācāṭa* is one whose speech is much censurable.”
Thus says Amara. The sense is that you possess the skill of an unprecedented artisan, having fashioned a stain upon the moon— your fame— which could not even have been created by Brahmā.
Therefore (*tat* = *tasmāt*), you do not exist; the meaning is that you are being killed right now.
By the phrase "by the beloved of Maithilī," it is indicated that Sītā has been recovered.
"Patanti," etc.

"Phalibhiḥ" means with those possessing barbs. Falling due to speed occurs because of the weight of the fruit; falling after a long time occurs because of the lightness of the leaf. Regarding "paścārdhaiḥ": even without [the word "vinā"].
By the rule "the substitution of *paśca* for the word *apara* must be stated when preceded by a word denoting a direction" (Pāṇini 5.3.28),
the word *apara* [is replaced].
The subsequent section first indicates his defeat by stating the futility of Rāvaṇa’s arrows. //59//
Regarding the phrase "in the axle" (*akṣe*) and so forth: "in the axle" means in the wooden piece fixed to the wheel.

The statement that they fall only in the places such as the axle within the chariot is because those very parts constitute the vital points (*prāṇasthāna*) of the chariot; this is the intended meaning.
By stating that even his shattered arrows shatter [the senses] such as the eyes, he indicates the velocity of Rāmabhadra’s shafts. //60//
"Rendered dark," and so forth.
*Śatāṅga* is a chariot intended for battle; [as it is said: "In a wheeled vehicle intended for battle, it is called a *śatāṅga* or a *syandana*."
"A chariot" (rathaḥ)—thus says Amara. "Śātamanyava" means belonging to Indra.
He states that there is no obstruction due to the comparison with rain; for this very reason, it vanishes from view.
Such is the statement. //61//
"Various," and so forth.
"Exceeds" means it becomes more than [necessary]. //62//

Regarding the passage beginning with "yad rāvaṇa," the construction is "by means of two arms alone. Since [the alternative] would be purposeless, it is better to have semantic significance even through a mediated connection (*vyavahitānvaya*). By this, he indicates an excellence in skill in combat. The result here is...
It takes the form of a counter-action to the action performed. By the word *bhaṭa*, craftsmanship (*śilpa*) is indicated.
Because there is a remedy with two arms for that which was created by twenty arms, it possesses tenfold power. //63//
"By twenty," and so forth; that which is performed by means of two arms is not exceeded by more than that.
"He does it"—this is a derisive remark. //64//
"Of him," and so forth.
*Kṣurapra* is a specific type of arrow. "He cut";
that is to say, he caused [it] to fall to the ground. For this very reason...
The chariot possesses the status of the point of departure (apādāna).
The humiliation of the pledge is its violation. "Vilakṣa" means ashamed; for that very reason, he is angry.
Regarding the phrase beginning with "dikpāla": "kalpāntasya" means of destruction; "karṇejapāḥ" means informers.

According to Amara: "A *karṇejapa* is a slanderer" (262); the suffix *ac* is applied by the rule "after *stamba* and *karṇa*, to the roots *rami* and *japi*" (263), and the non-elision (*aluk*) of the locative case ending occurs according to the rule "after a consonant or a word ending in *a*" (264). *Avagrāhiṇaḥ* means obstructors. [From] Rāvaṇa...

Due to fear of Rāghava, whose efforts are never in vain, the world-elephants have their rutting dried up; yet, because of the certainty of his slaying [the demon], Indra experiences the rise of rut from joy, and Paulomī finds the cessation of her sorrow. //66//
"Videha," and so forth;
"sākṣī" means one who knows directly.
"In another birth" means in the state of being a deity. "Causing a meeting" means bringing about a union; by this, he expresses the absence of danger. //67//
"By one alone," and so forth. "The healer of the worlds"—the worlds (*jaganti*);
making them healthy (*ullāghāni*), that is, removing their mental afflictions (*manoroga*); the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmani*). (266)
"Ullāgha means 'freed from disease,'" according to Amara.

"Ko'pi" means "beyond the reach of speech. "Nivāta" means "impenetrable by weapons," and "kaṅkaṭa" means "armor"; "nivāta" [also] refers to a shelter or a windless place, [as well as that which is] impenetrable by weapons.
And "varma" means armor; thus says Amara: "uraśchadaḥ, kaṅkaṭakaḥ, ajagaraḥ" (Amara-kośa 2.8.64). "Yadi nāma" = oh! "Yadi nāma" is used in the sense of wonder.
"Some" refers to Vardhamāna. Or, it refers to a change in nature, as in: "If a Brahmin is indeed a fool, how [could he be otherwise]? (271).
Vardhamāna:
(272) It is a marvel that there is a thousand wounds from a single arrow;
this indeed is a transformation of the natural state.
The sound "sīt" is the sound of the falling stream. "By Māhendra" indicates the cause for a thousand paths.
By the word "hero," he expresses the absence of despondency. //68//

"Sītā," and so forth. The sense is that [he becomes] possessed of sin through mere mental resolve (*saṅkalpa*) alone, and not through physical action. This is the reason for his being subject to execution. By "striking" (*ghātena*), [it refers to] wounds (*vraṇānām*) that have become manifest (*rūḍhānām*), i.e., those that have appeared.
*Arbudas* are types of calluses.
Their number is four because Airāvata has four tusks; regarding this, Māgha says: "Together..."
With Śakradantin, he entered a battle involving four tuskers; thus [it is said]. (69)
"Child," he said; thus, even for a child, the use of the word "prauḍhakarma" (one of mature deeds) is a refined expression.
Regarding "traivikrama" and so forth:
*jīvitavyam* means that life itself is the knowledge (*vidyā*), with the suffix *-tavya* used in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāve*); [the phrase refers to] the completion of that [knowledge].

*Lipiḥ* is the arrangement of letters indicating completion; Amarasimha states: "The term *lipi* refers to the arrangement of written letters" (2.8.275). The sense is that by observing the discus (*cakra*), it is known that there is no sustenance for the Rākṣasas. Thus, [it is called] *Sudarśana*.

The masculine gender [of the word *arā*] is optional because it belongs to the *ardharca* group (Pāṇini 2.4.31). The state of being shattered into spokes (*arāṇām*) is due to the hardness of the chest.

By the word *tuṣāra* (frost), particles are indicated. The ornament is one abounding in those particles of light that exist within the shattered lattices of petals; by this, he expresses its non-obstructive nature. //70//
*Hastavattā* means possessing strength;
*dīpyamānasya* means of one who is enraged.
Regarding the phrase "placed by oneself" (*svavinihita*) and so forth: it is because wounds from weapons themselves constitute the ornaments of a hero.

"Jesting with necklaces. Regarding the word "on their necks": the sense is that being enraged, he tore apart even those that were freshly made and exceedingly delicate, as if they were merely from his own chest. //71//
"Discourse with heroes" means battle; "defiance" means pride.
"Curiosity is filled" means it appears like a pet bird kept in a cage.
"Rising and falling," and so forth;
by the lifting and setting down of his feet, the earth becomes elevated and depressed, [reflecting] the jewels upon his hoods.
Due to the power of its manifestation and concealment, it possesses the nature of lightning by virtue of its momentary luminosity,
and there is also the instantaneous destruction of darkness.

The instrumental case in *niḥśvāsaiḥ* is used in the sense of a characteristic mark (*upalakṣaṇe*). (278) The boldness of the breath arises from the excessive weight resulting from the state of standing. *Ajani* means "was born" (*jātaḥ*);
the suffix *ciṇ* is applied in the sense of the agent according to the rule *dīpajana-* (Pāṇini 3.1.61). (279) //72//
"Rakṣovikṣobha," and so forth. *Vikṣobha* means leaping; it refers to the agitation of crocodiles due to the splashing of the water.
Alternatively, the reading is *vyakta*.
"Mātaṅganakrāḥ" refers to crocodiles in the form of elephants. "Krodhaḥ" (anger) arises from the perception of them as rival elephants.

"Gurutarām" (heavier) is said because the earth, though supported by nine [elephants], remains situated upon this very [elephant]. By the words beginning with "aṅgaireva" (by the limbs alone), [it is shown that] even that which is elevated is brought to a state of subordination.

The phenomena have been explained. The sinking of the limbs, beginning with the head, into the throat and other regions is due to the excessive weight. Regarding the term *atipīvnā* (by one who is excessively corpulent), it refers to one who is very obese; this is based on the word *api* in the rule *anyebhyo 'pi dṛśyante* (Pāṇini 3.2.101).

Because the word is intended to convey the deviation [of the meaning] from all adjuncts (*upādhi*), the suffix *kvanip* is applied to the root *pibati* even when it is not preceded by an upapada in the vernacular (*bhāṣā*). By the rule "ghumāsthā," etc., the substitution of *i* for the vowel does not occur. However, the concealment of the expansion of the hood is, in reality, [a property] of the body even now.

Because of its vastness. The instrumental case in "dehena" is used in a figurative sense (upalakṣaṇe). At that time, [the serpent], eclipsing—that is, surpassing—the "parīṇāham," which is the width or expansion, of the hoods. The word "phaṇān" refers to the hoods.
The meaning is "bending"; otherwise, because the hoods would be submerged within it, they would simply be crushed by the excessive weight—this is the intended sense.
The lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule: *upasargasya ghañyamanuṣye bahulam* (Pāṇini 6.3.122).
This is the "seen" (dṛṣṭa),

because that which is not directly perceived— the remainder— is made to appear as if it were directly perceived through the description of specific characteristics such as its state of being broken by an excessive burden of earth, its configuration, and its genus.

This is indeed an ornament; as it has been said: "That which is described according to its location, its time, and its form—whether it be perceptible or imperceptible—is considered 'seen' (dṛṣṭa), like something actually witnessed. (286) //73//
"He meditates," and so forth; for the attainment of the fruit occurs by that alone.
"Adhītān" means those [scriptures] studied up to the point of comprehending their fruitful meaning. By this, [the greatness of] Rāma's...

Victory has been indicated [by the word] "from the son of Gādhi. By the use of the ablative case (*apādāna*), the complete transmission of the science of missiles (*astravidyā*) to Rāma is indicated. For Rāvaṇa, however, there was only instruction and not formal study; this very fact indicates his lack of victory.

From this point until the end of the verse, "The ten-faced one slowly approaches" (287), there is the dramatic element named *prarocanā* (prologue/inducement), consisting of a statement regarding the future victory of Rāma and the defeat of Rāvaṇa as if they were already accomplished. As it has been said: "By means of a statement of what is established..."
"An incitement (prarocanā) should be indicative of what is to come. //74//
The phrase beginning with "yathā bhuvana" means: I conjecture that a manner has arisen by which the worlds are shaken in such a way. The phrase beginning with "tāmisra" [is explained as follows].
Because Rāghava was mentioned first as the one who counteracted the Tāmisra weapon, and given that the Tāmisra weapon belonged to Rāvaṇa while the Pāśupata belonged to Rāma,
[it follows that] Rāvaṇa’s...

The supreme state of being oppressed and the supreme state of being the oppressor of Rāghava have been indicated by the verse beginning with "kṛtapratikṛtīnām" (of those who have performed and returned deeds). Regarding Kākutstha, [the thought is] "I must conquer," while regarding Rāvaṇa, it is "I must die."
Thus ends the Rāmāyaṇa; and this [work],
through the sequence of its unfailing and efficacious resolve, results from the certainty regarding one's own victory or defeat.
"Viśikhamukha," and so forth. "Āṭopa" means agitation; he becomes weak.
He states the reason for this with the words "yaddaivatam," etc. [Regarding] "raghupateḥ" and "daśamukhasya."
Thus, with the intention of expressing a general relationship (*sambandhasāmānya*), the genitive cases take the place of the locative and ablative.

For here, by means of the two words *kṣipati* (casts aside) and *upadadhāti* (places down)—which denote actions indicative of disrespect and respect, respectively—the absence and presence of devotion toward the deities are shown; and by those [two],...
Victory and defeat by means of the bow have been indicated;
as it has been said: "In respect of a mantra, a sacred site, a twice-born, a deity, an astrologer, a medicine, or a teacher—wherever such a conviction exists, there success is attained."
Such is she. (291) //75//
"Whatever was cut," and so forth. By this, Rāvaṇa’s extraordinary enthusiasm is expressed; for one who has resolved upon his own death, such an excellence of prowess is thus imagined.
From here onwards: "His breath having departed, exceedingly difficult to bear..."
The section ending with "dehabandhaḥ" (292) concerns the state of pathos (*karuṇa*) due to Rāvaṇa’s succession of calamities; [the following] takes the form of pacifying that contradiction.
Śakti (power) is a constituent element (aṅga); as it has been said: "Śakti is the pacification of contradiction" (293). //76//
"Aye, 'perception of sound' and so forth. Perception (*upalambha*) means knowledge (*jñāna*);

its "instigating action" (*pravarttaka-karman*) is the activity of speaking (*abhivadanavyāpāra*) in the form of "whatever has been done" (verse 294), which indicates the destruction of Rāvaṇa. For this very reason, there is gratification (*prīṇana*).
A tumultuous noise behind the scenes.
This clamor here arises from the musical instruments of the monkey host, who are delighted by the fall of Rāvaṇa.

"How so? and so forth. It is that in which there are harsh sounds, like the throat-sounds of Viṣṇu who has assumed the deceptive form of a lion (*kaṇṭhīrava*), and *kāhalās*—specific types of war-trumpets.

In the word *nirghoṣe*, [it refers to] the expulsion and so forth. Regarding *prajānām*, "breaking the *koṣṭha*" means the bursting of the belly; Amara states: "The word *koṣṭha* in the masculine means the interior or the belly" (295). Thus, it means the breaking of the treasury of the subjects (*prajākośabhaṅgam*).
In the reading, "the destruction of the cosmic egg"; "at an improper time" means at a non-occasion; [this applies] to all beings or to the egg itself.

Because destruction is a property belonging to the end of a kalpa, the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is applied according to the rule "propābhyāṃ samarthābhyām" (Pāṇini 1.3.42). He describes that very property of being subject to the end of a kalpa with the words beginning with "kālakūṭa," and so forth.

"As if smeared" (*upadigdhair iva*) means as if anointed, because they cause the world to faint; the sense is that the worlds die simply by hearing his roar. He "remembers" (*smarati*) Bhairava, who is Kālarudra;
the genitive case is used for the object according to the rule beginning with *adhīgartha* (Pāṇini 2.3.52).
The recollection of Bhairava arises from a resemblance to the sound [of the drum]; the sense is that this occurs through the delusion that it is the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*).
"With divine weapons," and so forth: having fought with those fierce [weapons] that cause terror to the three worlds beginning with the earth, together with himself—
The word "Rāma" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. His head is like the sun because it is red with rage.
"Śikhā" means the fruit itself; the pedestal (pīṭha) is for the purpose of yoga, and [the deity] is upon that.
By the word "astra," its presiding deity is indicated.

*Avakīrṇaḥ* means scattered or strewn. *Vīraśayyām* refers to the battlefield; its status as the object [of the verb] is established by the rule *adhiśīṅsthā* (Pāṇini 1.4.46). For one who is exhausted by battle lies down upon it. //77//
*Prakāṇḍaḥ* means "excellent";
it is a compound formed according to the rule *praśaṃsāvacanaiśca*. *Paryavasitaḥ* means "dead," so to speak.
"Broken," and so forth:
*gandhapradhānaḥ* means "one for whom fragrance is primary"; *sindhuraḥ* means "an elephant"; the sense is "perpetually intoxicated. Regarding *śaśvat*:
whenever he conquered, at that very time...
The meaning is that he writes. To him who has composed this series of letters using those very pearls—
[the moon] which possesses a terrifying nature because, by capturing Indra and the other gods, it destroys the arrangement of the abundant ornaments of their beloveds.
Of the arms. //78//
"Steadfast," and so forth.
By the word *nija* (own), Śeṣa is meant.

Her bending [of the earth] is due to her being pressed down by the earth whose middle was depressed because of the excessive weight of the headless trunk of Rāvaṇa, which had fallen violently; for this very reason—

And there is a rising of the world-regions situated at the extremities; for when the center sinks, the ends rise up. Precisely because half of the earth's burden has been removed, [the suffering] caused by that excessive burden [ceases].
Because all coiling has been removed, he holds the circle of hoods with a support in the form of a body that is contracted in the front half;
for otherwise it would be impossible to hold them. The term *ādhāraka* is used here in its own primary sense (without a secondary suffix).
Who? (302) *Kādraveyāḥ* = the offspring (*apatyāni*) of Kadrū, namely the serpents (*sarpāḥ*); [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied after feminine stems [ending in long vowels]. (303)//79//
"Surpassing all intelligence" means that it is not only his conduct,
but even his death [surpasses all]. This is the intended meaning.
"Moves," and so forth.
"Conquers"—one who conquers is a *jetṛ*;
that which is itself a conqueror is *jaitra*, with the suffix *aṇ* used in its own sense (*svārthika*). "Where" means when Rāvaṇa, in whom [the world] moves, is present.
Just as iron bands are the supports for a pillar fearing to split, so too are the serpents the supports for Śeṣa; this indeed is the utility of the lord of serpents' hoods for his serpent-soldiers.
The shaking of the mountain was caused by the placement of Rāvaṇa’s foot; "vyatighaṭṭanena" means by friction.

*Ulbaṇāḥ* means manifest sounds. *Jalpākībhiḥ* means by those who are habitually talkative; the suffix *ṣākan* is applied according to the rule *jalpabhikṣa*(Pāṇini 4.1.19). By means of the sound of rubbing jewels, "talking" is metaphorically attributed to the hoods [of the serpents]. //80//
"Having drawn aside": she will become frightened by the sight of the headless trunk (kabandha); this is the drawing aside.
Here, *kāku* refers to a particular modulation of voice born of grief; "kāku is a feminine modification [of the voice]."
"Sound" (*dhvani*) is [defined] as being caused by grief, fear, and so forth—thus says Amara.
"A woman of excellent complexion" (*varavarṇinī*) means an excellent woman; "an excellent woman is a *varavarṇinī*"—thus says Amara.
Thus says Amara.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bhūyiṣṭhāni": *cāritra* means devotion to one's husband (*pātivratya*); she is the presiding deity (*adhidevatā*) of that, or she is one for whom that itself is the deity.

The word *api* indicates a contradiction: because he has ten faces and twenty arms, [the husband] enjoys the pleasure of union with many women as if with this very one alone; thus [it is said] of the devoted wife (*pativratā*).
The resolution of the contradiction regarding the numerous kisses and the many-armed embrace [is as follows]: *ekāvalī* is a single-string necklace, a specific type of *hāra*;
Amara states, "the *ekāvalī* has a single string" (308). [This refers to] the one who possesses the nature of speech, of that which was promised.
Because she did not offer a necklace fashioned from the pearls of Gaṇeśa’s frontal globe,
is it fitting for Sleep to feel passion— that is, attachment— for her? So [he asks].
The meaning is obtained from the sound [of the words].
The sense is that there is no happiness for one who is burdened by debt.
From this point until the end of the passage, "he brought [it] to a state of hardness" (309).
Because it takes the form of a praise of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, who are worthy persons, this is the dramatic element named *prasaṅga*;
as it has been said: "The glorification of a superior person is *prasaṅga*. (310)
Thus [ends the section]. //81//

The compound *cakṣuḥśrotrasya* follows the rule of singular treatment for parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅgaikavadbhāva*). The statement that it is impossible to see or hear is an expression of the excessiveness of suffering.
Regarding the phrase "of those who have retaliated" and so forth: even for an enemy who has been retaliated against, there is suffering.
The meaning is that it causes great distress. "Aha ha" is used to express distress and wonder. "Not even a little," and so forth;
[this refers to] Maṇḍodarī, who, despite being honored by Indra and the other gods, has come to such a state.
The meaning is that for Kṛtānta (the God of Death) acting, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be done.
He describes her majesty itself with the words beginning "vandāru-vṛndāraka... and so forth.
Vandāravaḥ means those who offer salutations; according to Amara, "vandāru" refers to one who salutes (312). Mālā means a crest-garland (maulisrak) (313). Karkaram means hard.
The meaning is "stupefaction" (*styāna*); [as for the word *karkara*,] Amara states: "The word *karkara* may also be used in the sense of 'hard'.
(314) [This occurs] due to contact with dust.
For water indeed becomes as if solidified. //82//
"Are led away," and so forth.
*Vallabhapālaka* means a protector of the king's favorite horses.
*Mandurā* means a stable for horses; as it is said: "A stable for horses, however, is called *mandurā*" (Amara-kośa 2.8.47).
Thus says Amara. Regarding the phrase "by those who were friends of Vibhīṣaṇa":
because he was devoted to the gods, the statement implies that his kinsmen were likewise so disposed. Regarding the phrase "intense shame": even for a protector...
Shame arises from being captured together with one's own subjects;
this begins here and continues until the conclusion of the act.
Because the gathering of the activities of one's respective duties by Vallabhapāla and others constitutes the limb called *ādāna*, it has been said: "*Ādāna*..."
"The summary of the task" (316). //83//
*Ciravāstavyam* means having resided for a long time; [the suffix] *tavyat* is applied to the root *vas-* in the sense of the agent, and it is also *ṇic*.
(317) *Saṃvargaṇam* means the gathering together of things that have been scattered here and there.
"O descendant of Pulastya," and so forth. By "kaṇikābhiḥ," meaning by small particles or traces, [the face] is "lakṣmaṇaḥ," meaning beautiful;
for Amara states: "One who possesses beauty is *lakṣmīvān*, *lakṣmaṇaḥ*, or *śrīlaḥ*. Precisely for this reason—

He whose shame has been cast off—either because he failed to obtain a chest-thrust, which is the ornament of heroes, even for himself as it was for Lakṣmaṇa; or because he remained unharmed while his younger brother was wounded; or because [he thinks], "While I am present, my younger brother..."
The sense is that the shame felt at being wounded has itself ceased because she herself is also wounded;
for [the wound] was present in her mind at the very moment of looking at his chest.
By means of a metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*), because shame is dependent upon it [the chest], that chest functions as the point of departure (*apādāna*).
*Naptā* means grandson (*pautra*); *vibhīṣaṇaḥ*. *Bhadrapīṭham* means a royal throne; "that which is a king's seat is called a *bhadrasana*."
"And that is a lion-throne," thus says Amara. Regarding "tuṣyat":
the grief caused by the death of Rāvaṇa has been pacified by the installation of Vibhīṣaṇa.
He whose wife is Jānakī is *jānakījāniḥ*; [this is derived] by the rule *jāyāyā niṅ* (Pāṇini 5.4.134). This indicates that he has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtakṛtyatva*). //84//
Regarding the term "act" (*aṅka*): it is so called because it consists of the direct manifestation of dramatic action, such as the consecration interrupted by the forest exile,
or the reunion with Sītā interrupted by the machinations of Rāvaṇa.
Furthermore, because it is joined with the words "Abhiṣeka" and "Jānakījāni," and because it is the locus for the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of various kinds of dramatic arrangements.
Thus ends the sixth act in the Anargharāghava-pañcikā composed by Viṣṇu, the son of Muktinātha.
